subtopic: LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE VALUE FOR DUTY ON IMPORTED GOODS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE VALUE FOR DUTY ON IMPORTED GOODS
speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of his recent statement in the house to the effect that any recommendations of the tariff board in regard to cotton textiles would not be considered this session, would the minister confirm his intention, as indicated in his budget speech, that section 35 of the Customs Act will be amended this session to provide that the value for duty on imported goods shall not be less than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE VALUE FOR DUTY ON IMPORTED GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement I made in the house on Tuesday in tabling the report of the tariff board on woollen yarns has no bearing whatever on the announcement I made in the budget speech on June 17 as to the intention of the government to introduce at this session an amendment to section 35 of the Customs Act for the purpose of introducing as a basis for value, as the hon. gentleman said in his question, cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit.
The announcement I made on Tuesday was by way of indicating the position of the tariff board with respect to the progress it has made with the very large reference to it of all the items in the textile tariff. The board has now made two reports, one on woollen fabrics and the one which was tabled on Tuesday on woollen yarns.
With regard to its inquiry into the tariff items in respect of cottons, the board has completed its hearings but I think it will be some time yet before the report is received and I was indicating in my statement that under these circumstances nothing by way of legislative action could possibly be expected at this session of parliament in relation to cottons, let alone other textiles, synthetics in particular, to which the board will be addressing itself in the remaining studies.
The amendment to section 35 of the Customs Act, as I indicated in the budget speech, will be introduced at the present session by my colleague the Minister of National Revenue.

The rate that has been set in each case, whether 3, 3J, 4} or 4J per cent, represents a realistic assessment of the cost of money in the market today in relation to borrowings with such maturities as have been set in the new conversion loan.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO COVER LOSSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the very serious rabies epidemic in Stormont and other parts of this province, has the minister considered the desirability of extending the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to cover compensation for the loss of domestic animals owing to rabies, as has been done in the case of brucellosis, tuberculosis and, I believe, in the case of foot and mouth disease?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO COVER LOSSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Animal Contagious Diseases Act provides authority for the payment of compensation only with respect to animals which are ordered slaughtered as a disease control measure to prevent the spread of the disease. This is the authority under which compensation is paid for animals ordered slaughtered if they are found, in the course of official testing, to be infected with brucellosis or tuberculosis. It is also the authority under which compensation would be paid for animals ordered slaughtered if they were infected with or exposed to such serious diseases as foot and mouth disease.
There is no authority in the act, and it is not the intent of the act, to provide compensation to owners of animals which may die normally from rabies or from any other disease.

Mr. Chairman, this item, of course, gives members of the house an opportunity to speak generally on questions within the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I wish to take advantage of that opportunity. Before doing so, Mr. Chairman, in a substantive way I should like to express my regret and the regret of members of our party over the resignation of the deputy minister of trade and commerce, Mr. Mitchell Sharp, and to express our gratitude-and I am sure all members of the house will join with me in this-for the magnificent, effective and unselfish service which he gave to the government through the civil service over so many years. I had the pleasure and privilege of being his colleague during part of that time, and therefore I am in a position to testify to the value of his unselfish service. I know he must have regretted leaving the civil service as much as we regretted seeing him go.
If Mr. Sharp had to leave, Mr. Chairman, he could not have been replaced by a better official than Mr. John English, who is now the deputy minister of the department and with whom I also have had the pleasure and privilege of working for many years as a member of the civil service. On my own behalf and on behalf of our party I would like to wish him well as he presides over the department in the capacity of deputy minister.
This item, Mr. Chairman, is related to the work generally of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and in preparation for the observations I want to make on that work I have been studying the annual report of the department. I have been looking at the report of the economics branch of this department. In the previous report for 1956 under this section "economics branch" there is this sentence:
During the past year, general economic conditions in Canada have been kept under review, and

a number of reports on various aspects of Canada's economic development have been prepared for official use.
This is the branch of the department, Mr. Chairman, which is responsible for the preparation of reports such as that famous so-called hidden report about which we heard last autumn and this spring; but in 1956 the reports of this branch were prepared for official use and official use only. For some reason or other, in the section of the 1957 report at page 53 dealing with the work of the economics branch there has been a slight change in reference to the duties of this branch, and this year the paragraph reads:
During 1957 general economic conditions in Canada were kept under review and a number of reports-
Including reports such as the famous hidden report.
-on various aspects of Canada's economic development were prepared-
And this is the change:
-mainly for official use.
I suppose it was necessary for the author of this report to include the word "mainly" to cover the practice of the Prime Minister in introducing to public attention some selected passages from a report of the economics branch that the branch said in the past was prepared for official use only.
I had hoped, Mr. Chairman, that in his review of the work of the department the minister might have given us the benefit of some information about the report for 1958, prepared by this branch on economic conditions in the country. It would have been very interesting to have received that information-perhaps more interesting, as it would have been more valuable, to have received it than it was last January and in the spring to have received selected passages from the previous report. If it was appropriate to have selected passages of that report made public in 1957, without any request from the house, perhaps it would have been even more appropriate to have had the information in the report for 1958 made public when it was requested by the house.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, it would have been helpful to have had an analysis of the economic situation as it was seen by the Department of Trade and Commerce, so that it might have been related to what the Minister of Finance had to say about it in his budget speech. However, that was not done.
In his review yesterday the minister emphasized, and quite rightly, the importance of foreign trade in our economy. Indeed, the magnitude and importance of our external
Supply-Trade and Commerce trade are shown, as he pointed out, by the fact that the figures have now reached well over $10 billion. That development of our external trade over the years until it reached this unprecedented figure in 1957, which as the minister pointed out was 2 per cent above the figure for 1956, and owing largely to the increase in the early part of 1957, must bring us all a great deal of satisfaction.
It must also bring some shadow of anxiety because of the realization of what it means in our dependence on markets outside of this country for not only our prosperity but our economic stability. In a sense it emphasizes that we are-I do not want to be misunderstood in the way I am putting this- hostages of other people's fortunes.
That is shown by the fact that about one third of our gross national product is now derived from our foreign trade, which reached a per capita figure in 1957 of $625, I think, a figure not exceeded in any country in the world except New Zealand, a country which is hardly comparable so far as industrialization is concerned.
It is also interesting to remark, and the minister mentioned it yesterday, that $7 billion of our $10 billion plus foreign trade comes from our trade with the United States of America. There is no difference of opinion among members of the house as to the desirability of diversifying, in so far as it can be done by natural, wise and economic methods, our foreign trade and broadening and deepening the bases of that trade. In 1958, in a time of recession, we are all very happy to know that our external trade is holding up so well. The minister pointed out-I think he used these figures-that in the first five months of this year our exports were about 1 per cent ahead of the same period in 1957, and that our imports were down something over 16 per cent from the comparable period of last year. Our imports from the United Kingdom are up 2 per cent, I believe, but our imports from the rest of the commonwealth are down about 11 per cent. Our imports from the United States are down even more than that. Because of that fact in the first five months of this year the deficit, as the minister pointed out, has been reduced from $514 million to $173 million, about one-third of what it was last year, and the deficit with the United States has been reduced from $660 million to $374 million.
But any satisfaction we can derive from the reduction of the unfavourable trade balance with the United States must be sensibly modified by a realization of the causes that have brought about the decrease in the deficit, because it is due not to an increase in our exports but to a decrease in our imports and it is not due to government policy. It is not

Supply-Trade and Commerce due to any shift from imports from the United States or other countries to Canadian production and purchases but is due primarily to the reduction in business investment in Canada, especially in machinery and equipment, a very important part of the import trade. That in its turn is due to the recession and the fact that our economy has slowed up so far as investment is concerned. There is less need for the capital goods that we had to import, particularly from the United States, when we were in a period of expansion and boom.
It is also true, as the minister pointed out yesterday, that this decline has been accompanied by a shift in the geographical distribution of our import trade. In 1957 the United Kingdom took about 8.8 per cent and in 1958 that figure increased to 10.4 per cent, whereas the United States share declined from 74.1 per cent in 1957 to 70.9 per cent in 1958. But again, while we may take some satisfaction from that shift, and I think we should, it is not due to government policy but to the recession and to the nature of the imports from the United States compared with the imports from the United Kingdom. The minister knows that our imports from the United Kingdom are mainly consumer goods. The level of imports of consumer goods is determined largely by personal income in Canada; and personal income, consumption and expenditure in Canada have, fortunately, been holding up very well in recent months.
On the other hand, our imports from the United States have been mainly capital goods and consumer durables and, as I have just said, the volume of their import is determined largely by the nature of investment in Canada. That has been declining as the demand for these goods in Canada and other countries is very sensitive to a change in business conditions, which change has taken place.
I have been talking about our import trade. There is also a shift in the geographical distribution of our export trade. The United Kingdom and the commonwealth are gaining relative to the United States but, as I am sure the minister will admit, that again is largely due to the increased assistance we have been giving to the Asian countries of the commonwealth under the Colombo plan; and while we may welcome that increase, we should not blind ourselves as to the reasons for it. The dominant factor, however, in our foreign trade remains our trade with the United States of America, and if conditions do not improve in the United States not only will our trade with that country decline but our trade with other countries will also decline, because those countries will feel the 

impact of any recession in the United States and that in its turn will affect their ability to buy from us.
The present situation may then be summed up by the following proposition. While it is true to say, as the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce expressed the same sentiment yesterday, that, to quote the Minister of Finance, "our trade deficit with the United States was reduced and our trade with the United Kingdom, the commonwealth and the rest of the world moved in the direction of more balanced relationships", it must be borne in mind that these changes and shifts in our trade picture have not been brought about by any systematic government policy but are the direct consequence of the current economic recession both in our own country and in the United States, and of the traditional nature of our trade relationships with the world but more particularly with the United States and the United Kingdom.
If our exports are holding up reasonably well, which is true and we all take satisfaction from it, it is important to analyse the reasons for that. The analysis made last night by the hon. member for Rosthern was a very simple one. He said that it was due to government policy and that disposed of the matter. Well, if he will study the export figures carefully he will discover, as perhaps he has already discovered, that our export trade is holding up largely because of the increase in three commodities, uranium, cattle and wheat. So far as uranium is concerned there has been a tremendous increase in our exports. This year they will perhaps be between $200 million and $300 million, whereas a year or so ago they were a very few millions and a few years ago they were almost nothing at all.
That increase is due not to the policy of the government but to the fact that the previous government managed to make an arrangement with the United States for the purchase of practically all the uranium we could produce at terms pretty satisfactory to the producers, and we are now reaping the benefit of that agreement. The agreement runs until 1962, and the minister must know that it is of the greatest importance to find markets for our uranium in other parts of the world. We are beginning that process, and it is very important to maintain it and expand the use of Canadian uranium for peaceful purposes.
So far as the cattle trade is concerned, I suggest to the hon. member for Rosthern that the government had about as much to do with the increase in cattle exports to the United States in the last year as the sultan of

Zanzibar, and I mean no disrespect to the sultan of Zanzibar. That increase, and it was a very formidable and desirable one, was due to a strengthened demand in the United States which in its turn was due first to the shortage of cattle because of the drought in that country and the need for cattle to restock United States ranges and ranches and, second, to the tremendous corn crop across the line which persuaded farmers and ranchers there to convert a lot of that corn into meat, for which purpose they were glad to have some Canadian cattle. While the government may have had very little responsibility for the increase in this cattle trade across the line, the government certainly has some responsibility for maintaining it. I am not so sure that that is going to be easy.
Would the hon. member permit an observation?
I might, but I do not think you would, Mr. Chairman. A question would be something else.
What I tried to establish yesterday-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret the necessity for informing the hon. member that his remark must be in the nature of a question which the Leader of the Opposition permits.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I wonder if the hon. member would tell us how we have been able to take advantage of this United States market if the policy of the government was so hostile that it turned the United States away from our market here?

Yes, I shall try to deal with that and explain why we were able when we were in power to lay the basis for this cattle trade across the border which, up until June 28 of this year, has resulted, the figures tell us, in 171,333 head moving across the border. To explain this you have to go back to 1947, when the Canadian tariff on fresh fruits and vegetables was bound under GATT. This was a very considerable concession to the United States, in return for which the United States had to make some concessions to Canada. One of those concessions, and perhaps as it turned out almost the most important of those concessions, was that the quota on Canadian cattle exported to the United States was raised to 400,000 a year. It was on the basis of that agreement that last year we were able to take advantage of this situation by increasing our cattle exports to the United States.
I would point out, too, that to preserve that concession, and it is a very important 57071-3-150
Supply-Trade and Commerce one and becoming so important that there are a great many rumblings of dissatisfaction amongst the producers in the United States, we have to maintain the concession we have given to the United States on fruits and vegetables. I believe the government is now negotiating with the United States- I will be informed if I am wrong-about an increase in the duties on fruits and vegetables. If an increase is made then the United States is entitled, in its turn, to concessions. Demands are being made already in Washington for such concessions in return for this concession on fruits and vegetables which is being requested by the Canadian government. One of the demands which is being most persistently made is for an increased duty and a reduced quota on Canadian livestock, and this at a time when livestock producers in Canada need all the markets they can get and when the United States, because of interest in the development of these markets, is clamouring now with greater force than previously to keep the cattle out. There is the problem.
The third main reason for our increased exports is our exports of wheat and flour. As was pointed out by my hon. friend last night and by the minister before him, last year we exported 282 million bushels.
No, 262 million.

Well, 262 million, and this year we are about to reach 300 million. By the end of the year I believe we may very well be over the 300 million bushel mark. This is a very substantial and very satisfactory increase indeed. But let us see how that was brought about. Perhaps a clue to it, in addition to what the minister no doubt would refer to as the aggressive sales policy of the Canadian wheat board-it was not so aggressive last autumn when we aked him about the desirability of taking steps to sell wheat to Australia-is given in United States figures. Last year their exports were 546 million bushels, and this year that figure has dropped to 400 million bushels. The reasons for our increase within that comparative figure are, first, the gifts and longterm credits we have made available to Colombo plan countries. The minister mentioned this yesterday, and I am not criticizing or quarrelling with that for one minute. Another reason is easier credit terms generally, whereas when we were in power we were able to sell our wheat for cash or commercial credit, except when we gave it away for relief or for Colombo plan consumption.
When we talk about increasing our wheat exports under the Colombo plan, as part of the Colombo plan arrangements we must not forget that the Colombo plan was established

Supply-Trade and Commerce and operated for capital and technical assistance, not on the basis of supplying consumer goods. When we had responsibility for operating the Colombo plan we found the Asian countries hesitant indeed about accepting consumer goods rather than capital goods.
Then another reason for the increase, as the minister pointed out yesterday, was the sales of wheat to Russia. He knows, of course, who made the agreement that made those sales possible. Then for the first time for a good many years there were some sales to China, and I shall have a word to say about that later. Another reason for the increased sales was the higher quality protein wheat in 1957.
Another very important reason, which is illustrated by the United States figures, is that the United States barter program, which was that aspect of their surplus disposal program which, perhaps along with tied sales, was causing us the most damage and about which we complained most, was modified. This modification began in April, 1957, as a result of assurances which we received from the United States government. At that time the United States government said they would not operate barter sales in such a way as to interfere with normal purchases of wheat by the importing country; that is one reason why the United States has not sold so much wheat in the current year.
While we all may take satisfaction, therefore, out of this increase in our export trade, perhaps it is just as well to analyse the reasons which brought it about. We still have, and will have for some time, surplus disposal problems. I suggest that the government should, if it has not already, give consideration to a co-operative arrangement with the United States for a joint approach, a continental approach if you like, to the problems of surplus disposal, especially of wheat. The government should give consideration also to international schemes for the utilization of surplus wheat and other foods, something about which they talked a good deal when they were in opposition and which, when we were in power, we had taken up at international conferences but with which we did not, in those days, make very much progress. Perhaps circumstances are such that now it will be easier to make effective progress.
There is also the proposal which might be very important for our wheat producers, for a NATO strategic food reserve. This is a matter which was brought up in the NATO council in previous years and in which other members of NATO did not show very much interest. At the end of last year the Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence- I am not sure whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned it but certainly the Prime Minister, Minister of National Defence

and Secretary of State for External Affairs- told the country that they had taken up at the December meeting of the North Atlantic council the feasibility-I am referring to page 2936 of Hansard for January 7, 1958-of implementing that proposal of creating a food bank, and that it would be studied, we were told, by the NATO council. In April, when the Minister of National Defence came back from the NATO defence ministers' meeting in Paris, he said that he also had advanced the proposal on strategic grounds of a food bank, a stockpile of wheat and that kind of thing; and he also said in April it was being studied.
I was very much interested in this proposal and the assurance we were given that it was being studied by NATO, because this might turn out to be a very important thing in the long run with regard to our wheat exports. So I was very much interested and somewhat disappointed to read the testimony of the United States ambassador to Canada before the senate foreign relations committee on May 16 last when, in answer to a question about this NATO food bank matter by a United States senator, he had this to say:
As far as the department is aware-
That is the United States state department.
-the Canadian government has made no detailed proposal in NATO or to the United States government that such a bank be established nor has any exploration of its possibilities taken place in NATO or the United States government.
Then he went on to say this:
Without receiving further details regarding the Canadian proposal it is impossible to tell how it might fit into NATO planning which has already been done, but this government will of course be glad to consider any detailed proposals which may be made in NATO by our Canadian friends.
We were told last December that it had been done. We were told in April that it had been done. I suggest that it is time the government begin it and make detailed proposals to NATO for this purpose, which they have talked about now for six months but which the United States government says has never been received at all in Washington or NATO.
I now want to say a few words about trade with China. The minister has been stimulating our curiosity in recent weeks on this subject, as indeed he and some of his colleagues stimulated our interest in a somewhat more ambiguous way during the election. It is true that wheat sales have been made to China, but I suggest that perhaps the government may have had very little to do with this matter. If the government wish to take active steps to encourage wheat sales to China or sales of any other commodity to China- and perhaps over the years though not immediately there may be quite a market there for Canadian products-I suggest they will

never make any progress if the Prime Minister talks in public as he did in this house on November 1, when he related the question of diplomatic recognition to the question of sales, and with regard to diplomatic recognition said this as reported at page 654 of Hansard of that date:
The attitude of this government is unchanged in that direction, and until such time as the people's government, the communist government of China, expiates its wrongdoing under international law there certainly will be no justification for the granting of recognition, as we see it.
That may be the policy of the government, and it is not in question at the moment in this particular debate. But to talk like that about a country to which you are hoping to sell goods does not seem to me to be very intelligent diplomacy. During the election campaign our position was stated very clearly, namely that we should do what we could as a government to develop our trade with China in respect of all goods which were not on the strategic list, and that for that purpose it would be desirable to send not merely a trade commissioner from Hong Kong to China but a governmental mission headed by a minister.
I ask the minister-and perhaps he will clear this matter up when he replies-what actually is the situation with regard to the strategic list for communist China. As he knows, over the years through a committee that meets in Paris-COCOM-lists have been agreed on with other NATO countries of goods which should not be exported to Russia and which should not be exported to China because of their strategic character. But there was a difference between the Chinese list and the Russian list. The Chinese list was more extensive than was the Russian list.
I have been trying for a good many months to find out whether that differential has been removed and, if so, whether the list of prohibited goods to China is now the same as the list of prohibited goods to Russia and whether that change, that co-ordination, has been agreed to by all the members of NATO. Until that change is made and until that differential is removed, it is going to be extremely difficult indeed for us to develop our exports to that country.
While over the years we may be able to build up an export trade to China, especially in agricultural products and in timber which were our two main exports in earlier years, we must not deceive ourselves that even under the most favourable conditions, this is something which will take place overnight. Perhaps within the next two or three years this may not be the market which will be the solution for an expanding export trade 57071-3-150J
Supply-Trade and Commerce but it is certainly worth developing. Far more important, as I have said, and the dominant factor in our trade, remains our trade with the United States.
I should like to say something about our United States trade relationships, more particularly in the light of the very happy visit we have just had from the President of the United States, who talked about these relationships. In this vital matter of relationships with the United States, whether political, economic or cultural, I think frank talk helps. If it is given in the right spirit it will not hurt; it will help to bring about an understanding of our mutual problems. It will help to clear away the cobwebs of some of the after dinner sentiments to which we are all exposed on occasion and which do not seem to me to be a very substantial basis for a sound Canadian-United States relationship.
So far as I am concerned, I have tried over the years to speak perfectly frankly but in as friendly a way as possible about our relationship with the United States. I have a very vivid memory of a speech I made in Toronto as far back as 1951, for which I was criticized very strongly by some people in this country who since that time have directed to the United States far more vigorous criticism that I was giving then. At that time in 1951 I ventured to say that the days of relatively easy and automatic relationships between our two countries were over especially, as I tried to point out, in the realm of economic affairs, and that our mutual problems in the future were going to be more complicated, more difficult and more numerous.
Nothing that has happened since 1951 has caused me to change my mind as to the validity of that forecast. In the years after 1951 I do not think anything I have said departed from that position in talks that I made in the United States or in Canada. I recall very well that in those days my hon. friend and some of his colleagues when on this side in the opposition used words which went further in criticizing the United States than we went on the other side. I remember some of them agreeing in those days, as perhaps they agree today, although I am not so sure now, when I said more than once in public that defence co-operation between our countries, which is not only desirable but is essential, and economic conflict are not reconcilable. I still think that is true.
The Prime Minister now does not like that sentiment. In this house he has charged me with using threats by talking like that and of wrongly trying to relate defence and economic relationships. I think defence is an important part of our economic and trade

Supply-Trade and Commerce relationships with the United States of America, and I do not mind him putting on the record again what I did say, so I can confirm that I stand by what I said. One of the things to which the Prime Minister has taken exception was a remark I made with respect to economic and trade matters while in San Francisco during the summer of 1957. So there will be no departure from my statement, and to show that I still stand by it, I will read what I said. I was talking about the demands of the United States for further tariff protection against Canadian imports and the resentment this was causing in Canada because of the already great imbalance in our trade with that country. I said:
The resentment caused in Canada by this process is increased when attempts are made to justify these demands for more protection on the ground that the requirements of defence make national self-sufficiency in certain commodities essential. This argument may well be valid in respect of certain vulnerable areas which might be closed to you as a source of supply in time of crisis or war. Surely it does not apply to Canada. We are the less impressed by the argument because on many other occasions we are told by other American authorities that defence can only be considered as a continental problem and dealt with on a continental basis. It is. I think, a simple, though significant, fact that any further restrictions on Canadian imports into the United States would make further defence co-operation more difficult. At least that is how I feel about it, and I am sure you would wish me to express my feeling in plain language as is customary when Americans and Canadians speak to each other.
That is what I said to the American Society of Newspaper Editors, and that is the way I feel about it. On July 10 the Prime Minister accused me in the House of Commons of trying to relate these two things in a wrong way and I would like to quote, as he did, what I said in this house on this matter in the debate on the reply to the speech from the throne. Just to prove that I stand by my remarks, I will quote not only the part of my speech which he quoted but I will add another sentence which he did not quote, as recorded at page 25 of Hansard for May 13, 1958:
We must naturally protect our interests when they are prejudiced by United States policy. We must, for instance, make it quite clear that the United States cannot expect full and complete co-operation in continental defence, which is desirable, if she treats us unfairly in her tariff and trade policies.
I also added the following sentence, which the Prime Minister did not quote:
But at the same time we must do everything we possibly and honourably can, to avoid economic conflict with the United States, which conflict would be bad for both countries and certainly disastrous for us.
That is exactly how I feel. Surely it is a good thing for the United States to know that in our view in this country the kind

of defence co-operation which we would like to have-full and complete-is not possible, as it should be possible when there is economic conflict. We will co-operate with the United States with respect to defence, irrespective of economic policy, because we must in our own interests, for our own safety and for our own security; but that co-operation will not be as complete as it should be if there is economic conflict alongside it. That is what I said, that is what I mean, and that is what I still stand by. I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he next gets up to speak whether he disagrees with that particular doctrine.
On July 9 last, when the President of the United States spoke in this house he honoured us, he complimented us, by speaking frankly, as I think we should speak to each other but without recrimination on either side. He said, and he was right, that frankness is the measure of friendship, and in his speech he said some things which were true and valid. I think he put some of the differences, especially the economic differences, between us in perspective and perhaps in a little better balance than had existed previously. But he was stating the United States case just as our Prime Minister when he goes to the United States states-and I hope he will continue to state-the Canadian case.
While we must respect what the President said and I think we must be complimented by his frankness, we do not need to agree with everything he said any more than we have to agree with the United States policy all the time. He did state the United States case with respect to their agricultural surplus disposal policy in a way which perhaps helped us more than we have previously been helped to appreciate the United States side of the picture, but I am afraid he did not remove all our doubts as to the wisdom of United States policy in this matter in so far as its relationship to Canada is concerned.
He raised the question of base metals, about which we are pretty anxious because the exports of these metals are so important to this country. Here I think we should pay tribute to the efforts of the administration in Washington to maintain the position in that respect by preventing action which would keep out our base metals and by endeavouring to fall back on stockpiling, something which will help their own producers without, we hope, hurting ours.
I suggest, however, it is not a tolerable position in Canadian-United States economic relationships when in time of crisis-and I am thinking back to the world war and to Korea-we are asked to bend all our efforts in this country to develop our natural resources and to produce strategic materials

and make them available for the common good, particularly for that of the United States. Then when we do this and the crisis is past these considerations seem to be, if not forgotten, at least diminished in the minds of those who previously persuaded us and we are told that only economic considerations, particularly the considerations of local producers, really govern domestic policy. If we are to develop resources of this kind for the common good in time of crisis, surely we cannot be left high and dry with respect to that development and that production when the crisis is over.
During the war we faced this problem and we tried to solve it. We solved it very successfully in wartime by setting up joint boards in Washington. I particularly have in mind a board covering base metals and materials called the combined materials board; and perhaps the time has come-and I have mentioned this before in the last two or three months-for the government to explore the possibility of once again establishing a joint raw materials board with the United States for the consideration of these questions. Perhaps this would be a very good subcommittee of the joint cabinet committee, either on economic matters or on defence matters, because this is certainly an important aspect of defence.
The President also dealt with the United States action in regard to oil imports. He tried to remove some of our worries on that score, and emphasized that in the action they were taking they hoped to cause a minimum of damage to Canadian producers. Then he had this to say, and I quote from page 2085 of Hansard:
We believe that to ensure adequate supplies of oil in an emergency, it is necessary that exploration to develop oil reserves be carried forward with vigour. This means a healthy oil industry throughout the continent and a healthy domestic oil-producing industry is vital to our national security.
Well, that is true; but I should like to substitute for that word "domestic" in the United States statement the phrase that a healthy "continental" oil industry is vital to our security. As I said in my speech in San Francisco, while it may be desirable for consideration of security not to be dependent on overseas sources of oil, you cannot use that argument in connection with continental production in North America. If defence is to be considered on a continental basis, then resources and material for continental defence must also be considered on a continental basis. Perhaps we are more aware of that necessity today than we were a week ago; because the events of this week must surely have driven home to people in Washington, London, Paris and Ottawa that in placing re-
Supply-Trade and Commerce liance on overseas sources, especially in the Middle East, for vital oil supplies one is resting on a very unstable foundation.
There was one other matter which the President talked about and which was probably also talked about a good deal more in private discussions. This was United States policy in regard to the exports by Canadian subsidiaries of United States firms to countries which are on the prohibited list as far as United States exports are concerned. As my hon. friend from Ottawa West pointed out yesterday, in spite of everything that has been said, we over here, at least, are still in some confusion as to the situation with regard to this very important matter, a matter which is not only of practical importance but of political importance, too, and which involves questions of principle and of national sovereignty.
I suggest the sooner we can get this matter cleared up the better it will be for relations between our two countries. Is it not an intolerable position that the United States should pass laws of extraterritorial application of the kind covered by this particular law, administered in such a way as to ignore the interests of Canada in her own trade? If in fact, as we have more or less been led to believe, the application of this law so far as Canadian exporters are concerned can be set aside by administrative action, I should hope that the United States administration would announce that they were going to adopt that policy with regard to such administration rather than merely suggest that every time there is a special Canadian case under this law consultations will take place.
There are a good many other things about which the minister talked. I am not going to deal with them all, because we will have a chance when the individual items of the estimates come up for consideration. I should however like to mention some of the omissions from his statement. There was, first, one very important omission. Perhaps this may not have been the right occasion for him to talk about the matter, but I hope he will rectify the omission before long. I refer to the menace of Soviet trade and economic policy to our own trade and export policy, and the ways in which we should meet it in concert with our friends, which is the only way in which it can be done. Perhaps a week ago we should have said that this menace was greater than the threat of military action.
There is no doubt whatever that in the last year or two a decision must have been made in Moscow to push ahead with an offensive on this particular front. We know the strides

Supply-Trade and Commerce the Soviet union has been making in export trade during the last two years and also with regard to aid, particularly to African and Asian countries. That aid in the last couple of years has amounted, I have been told-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-to the figure of about $2 billion. This constitutes a real problem for Canada and the other free countries. It is something we will have to do something about.
Then there was another notable omission, an omission which was noted by my hon. friend from Ottawa West, namely the way in which commonwealth economic questions were dealt with, or rather were not dealt with. We did not hear very much about the results of the trade mission of last autumn to the United Kingdom. By this time I should have thought it would have been possible for the minister to be able to say something in concrete terms about the result of that mission, more particularly whether the govpi-nment itself has increased any of its purchases over which it has control and diverted any of them from the United States to the United Kingdom. We heard very little at all about diversion. Perhaps diversion has now disappeared as an element of government policy.
We heard nothing-and it was a very important omission-with regard to the United Kingdom offer of free trade. The hon. member for Rosthern had something to say about this last night, and it was a very interesting observation indeed that we were all free traders. Then he went on to explain what he meant. I wish the spokesmen for the government would say the same thing in the same terms on the eve of the commonwealth economic conference.
Whenever we bring this up in the house we are always asked what our own policy is, and that is a fair enough question. The hon. member for Peel is not here today to ask it of me or it would have been asked before now. Our policy in this matter, as a party, has been stated more than once. It is that immediately that this offer was received we should have told the United Kingdom government that we would give it immediate, sympathetic and full consideration, and we would start discussions with the United Kingdom government in respect of it on the governmental level to explore the possibility of working something out. Whether or not the government has done that I do not know; they have never given us any reason to believe they have had any talks of any kind in respect of this very important offer.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? With regard to the statement of the policy of his party concerning

this offer, which he has mentioned several times and which he has now put on the record, he has based that on a resolution passed at the conference of the Liberal party last January. Would the hon. member put that resolution on the record in full, including the last two sentences in which I am particularly interested?
We will be glad to do that. We will put it on the record in the interests of the discussion.	*
In full?
Of course. Our resolutions are published, unlike the resolutions of the last Conservative party conference. They are there for everybody to read, and we will stand on them.
They hid their resolutions.

I thought the minister was going to ask me what I meant when I said we would start discussions with the United Kingdom government. That would have been a good and reasonable question. I have in mind exactly the kind of discussions which the United Kingdom government is holding with European countries in working out a free trade area with the continental European countries. The move to work out a customs union on the continent was a very important development, and other European countries who were not included in this union had to make up their minds whether they would associate themselves with it in some form of free trade area or whether they would stand aloof.
The Scandinavian countries, Ireland and the United Kingdom and others were concerned with this. The United Kingdom took the stand that they must try to associate themselves with the customs union by working out a free trade area. They have been discussing this matter for a couple of years now, and that, I suggest, is what we should be doing at this time about the United Kingdom free trade offer.
In these European discussions there should be no delusion in anybody's mind about the difficulties in the way of working this out, and I think it is yet too early to say whether or not they are going to be successful. But they are trying to meet the objections to the establishment of a European free trade area by laying down provisions which would ensure that as the area is built up over the years-because they are going to take their time over it-the position of particular industries inside the free trade area would be considered, and the impact on them would be cushioned over 15 or 20 years.
That kind of approach would, of course, have to be made by any Canadian government

in talking to the United Kingdom government about a free trade offer. I suggest however to the minister that there is nothing which is of more importance in the economic problems facing this country or this government than arrangements which would have to be made for Canadian association with this European free trade area.
When I say that if we had been in power we would have begun discussions with the United Kingdom over these free trade proposals, I do not for a moment believe that any bilateral arrangement between the United Kingdom and Canada would be enough.
Even this kind of bilateralism is inadequate. Therefore we would have to do our best with the United Kingdom and with our friends to expand those arrangements over the whole of the Atlantic area. This means trying to bring in the United States.
Now, I have no illusions about the difficulty of this, or about the obstacles in the way of solving those problems of Atlantic freer trade. But, Mr. Chairman, this is the day of vision, and I do not know any more important or any greater vision, apart from building up our own country, than trying to build up the Atlantic area as a free trade, politically co-operating and defence area. Surely there could be no more important Canadian policy at this time, political or economical, than to take the initiative in that regard.
Here again I know something about the difficulties in trying to convert NATO, for instance, into something other than a defence organization. I have attended a good many NATO meetings, and at every NATO council meeting I ever attended we brought up the question of implementing article II. I confess we did not make much progress, very little indeed.
I also sat on the committee of NATO which was charged with the duty of working out recommendations which would convert NATO from a defence organization into a political and economic co-operative organization through consultation in non-military matters. We produced a report on this which is a pretty good report, but it is much easier to produce reports than to implement them, as indeed we pointed out in our own report. However, circumstances have now changed. During the last two years since that report was prepared the Europeans themselves have begun to build up their own political and economic area.
One of these days they will perhaps-I hope this is true-have completed that process. If they do, I hope they will do it in a way which will not shut out North America because, as the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have
Supply-Trade and Commerce pointed out, it is absolutely essential that that European area be a low-tariff area, if we can make it so. Any other kind of European free trade area bodes no good for us. Therefore we should make, and I am quite sure we are making, our influence felt in Europe to ensure this does not happen. But our influence in this matter would be far greater if we could also take a lead expanding the proposed European free trade area into Atlantic freer trade.
I do not know anything more important, as I have said, than a Canadian government initiative along these lines. I do not know any more important vision before us-except the vision of building up our own country, and the two are related-than that of developing a great Atlantic free trade area, especially at this time when the free world countries, especially the Atlantic countries, must get closer together economically or politically or they are going to fall apart.
NATO has been the sheet anchor of our defence and our security in the last 10 years, but NATO is not going to survive, I am afraid, merely as a military alliance. Now that the Europeans have begun the process, now that the Russians are emphasizing the necessity of continuing that process-they very often are the people who make us aware of things like this-I hope the government will take very seriously indeed the desirability of not only discussing with the British a free trade area, but of broadening the basis of this discussion to include all the NATO countries and perhaps even as many commonwealth countries as would come into such an association. If we can do that, not only will we have laid a better and stronger foundation for our trade and economic policies in the future, but we may have laid a stronger foundation for peace and security in the world.

I wonder
whether I might ask the Leader of the Opposition a question purely for information. He made an interesting reference to a form of continental plan for the development of resources of oil and gas, or oil in particular. I wonder whether he was referring to the often mentioned plan of considering the resources as a unit? If so, would he not feel that conceivably, based on the small percentage that Canadian crude represents in such a continental plan, our resources of oil might represent even a smaller unit or proportion than it does today?

Yes. If I may deal with that point, I appreciate that particular danger and I did not have that particular device or procedure in mind when I talked about the joint materials board. I had in mind the

Supply-Trade and Commerce mechanism we developed during the war when it was necessary to produce raw materials on a continental basis for war purposes, quickly and efficiently, and when it was necessary to allocate that production over the whole of the continent, indeed, not only the whole of the continent but over the whole of the anti-Nazi world at that time. What I had in mind-and I go no farther than this at the present time because it requires a good deal of thought and study in working it out-is the kind of joint materials board such as the one we had in Washington at that time so that those problems, especially concerning base metals, oil and supplies of strategic materials, could at least be considered by both governments through their representatives on a continental basis. When one government felt that is was being unfairly treated, or that some development taking place in the other country was prejudicing a development in Canada, there would be this kind of mechanism to which to appeal.
That can be done now through governments, and of course it is being done, but perhaps it would be of some use to have a permanent committee. I know we talk a lot about boards these days, and sometimes boards are excuses for inaction rather than mechanisms for action, but perhaps it would be useful to have that kind of board, if you like, as a joint subcommittee of governments which would be meeting almost continuously, as it used to meet in Washington during the war, where those problems could be threshed out. But I did not have in mind the detail which my hon. friend mentioned in regard to oil.
As far as the second part of his question is concerned, I have only this to say. Perhaps he will agree with me, but perhaps he will not, that surely the economic way to develop our oil resources in western Canada would be to exploit the northwestern and western United States markets. That is the way it would be done in a rational world and we would get our oil supplies in the east where we could import them most economically, from overseas or from Venezuela, or from any other country. Perhaps that is the way it should be done in a rational world; but if this world, indeed if this continent, is not to be rational and if Canadian producers are prevented from access to that United States market and thereby prevented from developing their production, then I suggest that any Canadian government would have no alternative but to see what it could do to market our oil in eastern Canada. That is not anything that a government would want to do on economic grounds, but it is something a government might have to do on national

development grounds especially if we are excluded from an economic market across the border.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister would like me to put on the record this Liberal resolution.
Yes; I have lost my copy of it.
Ours was printed and is available.
I will be glad to send you 50 copies for distribution to your members.
I have a large wastepaper basket, but go ahead.

The resolution reads:
In that perspective-
Perhaps I should read the whole thing.
Don't read the whole booklet.
I will not read the whole book but I will read the resolution on trade, and I hope my hon. friends will be able to refrain from cheering as I read:
Cheering or jeering?

No, I said "cheering". I read:
The Liberal party has always favoured policies which promoted the expansion of trade on a multilateral basis, and under Liberal administration Canada's trade attained unprecedented volume. From a total of only slightly more than a $1 billion in 1934, our trade increased to more than $10 billion in 1956.
In view of the success of these policies-
Oh, oh.
Well, an increase from $1 billion to $10 billion may be considered as evidence of some success.
Normal growth.

Normal growth because of intelligent government policy. I continue:
1. The Liberal party believes that the prime object of Canadian trade policy should be to continue to increase exports as much as possible and to widen the geographical basis of our external trade. This expansion, not diversion of trade, is the only policy compatible with sound, rapid economic development and with increasing productivity and living standards.
2.	The Liberal party believes that Canada should continue, within the framework of international agreement, to seek the reciprocal removal of trade restrictions in the world and to prevent economic isolationism.
3.	The Liberal party also believes that to assure the security of the free countries we must work toward a close interdependence of our economies to gain greater opportunities for trade, full employment, greater productivity and higher living standards.
4.	In that perspective, a Liberal government would give immediate, sympathetic and detailed consideration to the British proposal for the gradual establishment of a free trade area between the United Kingdom and Canada and would take

Into account both the new opportunities that might be opened for Canadian industry and the importance of maintaining existing industries and living standards in Canada.
That is perfectly reasonable, and that is exactly what is happening in the development of the European free trade area today. That is exactly the way they are proceeding, because these transitions cannot be made overnight and they cannot be made without cushioning the shock in respect of industries which in the long run might benefit but which in the immediate future might be hurt.

I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. Yesterday I asked a question of the hon. member for Ottawa West which, by the way, was not recorded correctly in Hansard. I was referring to world war II, not world war I. I said that prior to world war II Canada had 40 per cent of the wheat market and in 1956 Canada had 25 per cent of the wheat market, and I asked why there was this decline in view of the Liberal government's trade policies.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Ottawa West is jealous of his right to answer that question asked by the hon. member yesterday. He has been doing some research work, and he will answer it immediately I sit down. The last paragraph of this very progressive and important resolution reads:
In the same spirit, a Liberal government would also consider the possibility of a co-ordinated program for the reduction over a period of years of trade barriers within the commonwealth and Atlantic communities.
We are very glad today, Mr Chairman, in July, 1958, to stand on that policy.
May I ask a question?

Now that we have had the resolution passed at the Liberal leadership convention of 1958 put on the records of the House of Commons, I wonder whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce would now place on the record the resolution on the subject of trade passed by the Conservative leadership convention in December, 1955.
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish to ask a question?

I should like to ask the Leader of the Opposition a question. In his speech he dealt with the export trade to the United States, including livestock. Then he read the Liberal policy and stated that the Liberals have always worked toward freer trade. I should like to ask him why
Supply-Trade and Commerce they did not obtain the removal of the embargo on Canadian cattle in 1946, when we could not ship our cattle to the United States and the price in that market was 30 cents a pound?
I tried to point out that in 1947 we did take action in that regard and made an agreement under GATT which made it possible to get into the United States market.
You could have done it two years earlier.

Perhaps I should answer the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. I did not understand the question when he asked it yesterday but I saw it this morning at the opening of the house when I got Hansard. I find that as reported on page 2329 of Hansard the hon. member asked this question:
Will he touch on the question why Canada had 40 per cent of the wheat market prior to world war I and has only 25 per cent of the world market now?
This morning he says that he meant world war II. In any event, the very short and simple answer is that there are three reasons. If he relates it to world war I he will have to recognize the development programs in Europe, particularly the extremely high protection put on wheat.
Before we get an unnecessary explanation, may I say that my question had to do with world war II.
Well, it is still the same thing.

For you
people.
I do not know what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert means by that.
You are living in the past.

From the hon. member's technique in the house I would assume that he has no appreciation of the problem of marketing wheat and its significance in the economy of this country. Perhaps he might refrain from interrupting until we deal with what I am sure the hon. member who asked the question will appreciate is a very important and serious matter to this country. I think the hon. member who asked the question asked it in a serious way and intended it to be treated seriously.
There is the whole question of the development of production in the European area. We recall the tremendous tariff protection,

Supply-Trade and Commerce indeed the virtual embargo, with respect to Canadian wheat imposed by certain governments in the immediate pre-war period in order to develop their production. We recall the development in Russia whereby Russia increased its production of wheat and used the weapon of trading wheat with certain countries in adjacent areas for heavy equipment which was needed, and by that device increasing her own wheat production.
In this morning's Montreal Gazette there is a Reuters dispatch from Moscow dated July 17 which is headed, "Red Wheat Hike". It reads.
The area under wheat in the Soviet union increased by 34 million acres between 1954 and 1956 and now is one and a half times as big as the area under wheat in Canada, the Soviet news agency Tass announced today.
The third and most important factor is the tremendous increase in the production for export in the United States of America. I think the hon. member will agree that that is the most important of the three factors. The subject is one that is worthy of a full length speech. There are two very short documents containing some interesting data on the subject and treating it in a more historical way. There is a little booklet published by the Canadian institute of international affairs entitled, "What's Happening to Wheat" by M. Western and R. Hedlin. It is a very small pamphlet. Then there is another rather thorough treatise on the subject. It is a thesis submitted by Mr. M. W. Menzies, who I believe is now an economic adviser in the Department of Finance. The thesis was written in 1956 for the University of London, and it deals with the Canadian wheat board and the international wheat trade. It is a very comprehensive and thorough document and contains all the historical developments.
It is a masterpiece.
I hope I have answered the question.
May I ask a supplementary question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Assin-iboia.

I think the house will agree that we have all been very patient and lenient about the number of questions that have been asked the previous speaker. I think he and his colleagues have been very generous in giving full answers to those questions. I listened with a good deal of interest yesterday to the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I was pleased to have this comprehensive review of the government's attitude toward trade with various countries.

It was a review of our experience and something of the outlook for the future.
The minister made a statement of which we were all aware, that during the current crop year there have been substantial increases in our exports of wheat. In this regard I am not going to follow the impression I received from the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition when he was speaking about it, that he wished to take away a substantial part, if not all, of the credit that might be due to the government for this improvement. I am quite prepared to give the government whatever credit may be due to them, and I think there is credit due them for having adopted policies which, if not entirely new, were certainly expansions of other policies and which have resulted in this improvement.
I hope the minister's statement that the coming crop year should equal the past one or perhaps even exceed it will be borne out by experience. I believe that if we can get our exports up from, let us say, the present 300 million to 350 million bushels as an annual target figure, even if we have larger wheat crops in the future than we have had in the past we will be able to liquidate the surplus we now have. I hasten to add, as I see the minister smiling when I ask for a further increase in exports, that I feel it is my job to keep setting a target for him so we will keep on improving. If crops are of average size or even less than that, according to the history of this country exports at the annual rate of 300 million bushels are enough to clear the crop.
There is another aspect of this matter which I believe should receive the attention of the minister immediately, and that is the whole question of the price the producer receives for the commodity. There are two important aspects of this subject, one sales and the other price. The minister has shown that there has been a substantial improvement in sales, but the same improvement does not apply to sales of barley or flax. In fact I believe there is no improvement, and that they are running at about the same figures as last year. There has been some improvement with regard to wheat.
I am wondering if the minister could inform the house, when he speaks, whether or not there is an application now before the board of grain commissioners by elevator companies for a further increase in their handling charges for grain. He will appreciate that any increase in the handling charges that might be allowed will come out of the producers' payment for wheat and reduce any subsequent interim or final payment.
I should like him to comment also on this aspect of the government's program, which was started by the previous administration,

namely the payment of storage costs on that quantity of wheat in excess of 178 million bushels in storage on July 31. Would he say whether, in the grain picture as it is now developing, the amount of storage the government will pay into the wheat board fund on account of this policy is likely to be reduced? I think that will follow as the surplus is moved to the markets of the world. When the government's payments into this fund are reduced, that will result in the wheat producers receiving an even smaller payment in the years ahead.
I noticed the other day a report in the press that the government's bond issue may result, and is likely to result, in an increase in the premium on the Canadian dollar. This would be another factor which would result in further deterioration in the price of grain. I am asking the minister, therefore, whether he can give us, when he speaks, the price picture and the price outlook so far as these important commodities are concerned.
I noticed with interest the minister's statement that exports increased in 1957 over 1956 by some 2 per cent. The minister seemed to me to be rather satisfied with what had been accomplished and with the general outlook. I believe that an improvement of 2 per cent in 1957 over 1956, in the light of all the circumstances, in the light of the needs of this economy, is in fact a rather dismal showing.
It is a record.

I know it is a record, and I
am going to have something to say about that. If we should keep on having a record every year of adding 2 per cent to our exports it means that we are falling down in the export field, because to increase our exports by 2 per cent, coupled with the statement of the Minister of Finance on previous occasions that the gross national product would probably go up by the same 2 per cent this year, means a continuing recession in this country. It is not good enough to have a 2 per cent increase, even though in dollar value this may be a record. Unless we are able to increase our exports by a much higher rate than 2 per cent we are going to have continuing trouble in our industries which depend on export markets.
The government has had some very nasty things to say about the previous administration. I always sit back and listen with a great deal of enjoyment when I hear government members tearing into the official opposition on the basis of their record. I think if the Minister of Trade and Commerce will look at the record of exports for the previous two years, as compared to the same time a year previous in each case, he will see that
Supply-Trade and Commerce in times of prosperity in this country our exports were increasing by a figure much in excess of 2 per cent.
May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I have in my hand some figures on the increase in total merchandise exports in recent years. I find that the Bank of Canada statistical summary shows that merchandise exports for 1957 stood at $4,935 million, an increase of $72 million over the previous year or 1.5 per cent. The merchandise exports in 1956 increased by $512 million over the previous year, or some 11.8 per cent. In 1955 merchandise exports increased over the previous year by $404 million or 12.4 per cent.
The point I am making is that while there was an increase of between 1 per cent and 2 per cent in 1957 over 1956 in commodity exports or merchandise exports, this was just a small part of the much larger increase that had prevailed in the two preceding years. I think there is a definite correlation between the very small increase in merchandise exports in 1957 and the very substantial unemployment this country has been facing.
The increase in the physical volume of exports which adjusts exports to a change in the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar, shows exactly the same trend. In 1954 the index for the physical volume of exports, based on 1948 equalling 100, was 109.6. In 1955 the index had gone up to 118.3 or an increase of 8.7. In 1956 the physical volume of exports was up to 128.3 or an increase of 10. In 1957 the index was up to 129.8 or an increase of only 1.5. Hence while there has been a moderate increase in 1957 it is a rather inadequate showing in comparison with that in previous years.
To me the disturbing part of the minister's statement is that he seemed rather satisfied with the 1957 volume of Canadian exports, and he seemed quite satisfied with the showing in 1958. He did not say to the house what is a fact, namely that our 1957 exports should have been higher and that the 1958 exports should be much higher than they are now. If the minister had been in the same frame of mind as his party was a year ago I think he would have had important plans that would result in a large increase in our exports. Instead, he was content all through his speech to take what seemed to be general satisfaction in the trade picture

Supply-Trade and Commerce as it now exists. In his opening remarks, as reported at page 2320 of Hansard, he said:
For the year 1957 a new record total was established in our commodity exports, amounting to almost $5 billion, or about 2 per cent above 1956, which in turn had been a peak year. Preliminary figures for the first five months of 1958 confirm a further improvement in our foreign trade, with total commodity exports for this period amounting to almost $2 billion, or about 1 per cent ahead of the corresponding period last year.
Then he went on to say:
Some of the reasons for this good showing-
He terms a 1 per cent increase a good showing. I would suggest that a 1 per cent increase is an inadequate showing and that very serious economic conditions will result in this country if we cannot get it above 1 per cent in the days ahead.
About a year ago now the government was making statements as to the effects which would flow from a commonwealth trade conference. When the commonwealth trade conference last year was concluded statements were issued on the wonderful results of this conference. From the statements that were issued at that time we thought a new era was dawning, but in the minister's statement today I see little attention given to the coming commonwealth trade and economic conference. He seems to take a rather conservative view, I would say, of what the results of that conference may be. As reported at page 2323 of Hansard he said:
We are looking forward to the commonwealth trade and economic conference in September in the hope that there will be a further expansion of markets within the commonwealth, a removal of trade restrictions and the development of a new approach to some of the major trade and economic problems facing the world today.
We find there very little in the way of a definite policy and certainly, to me, no indication that the government really expects this conference to do a great deal for Canada. I do not know how the government can expect the conference to have any great success when, in advance of the conference, the government has announced that it would increase tariffs on certain goods coming into Canada from the United Kingdom. It would seem to me that the government announced in advance that it was putting roadblocks in the way of this coming commonwealth trade conference.
You hope.
What was that statement?
You hope.
That is not true, and the hon. member should not be making a statement like that.
Then why all the gloom?

In his remarks the minister has said-and his colleagues have indicated it also-that these tariff increases are going to take place. When it was announced in Canada that this government was increasing tariffs the press reports in Great Britain, as far as the conference was concerned, were very disturbing indeed. Some of the most influential publications in the United Kingdom questioned what would come of this conference in the light of the restrictive trade practices which this government had indicated it would follow.
The minister also, in my opinion, seemed to brush over rather lightly, though he spent some time on the subject, the common market being set up in Europe. I think this common market, if Canada is not associated either with it or with the free trade area, could have some very bad effects for Canada; and I do not make that statement on my own, for it has been made by some of the most prominent farm organizations in this country. They say it is clear to them that the common market which is to be set up in Europe might be disastrous as far as exports of wheat from Canada to Europe are concerned.
I hope the government will some day tell us what is its policy as far as the United Kingdom free trade offer made last year to Canada is concerned, and I think the government should now be considering, with the United Kingdom and other European countries, how Canada can associate itself with the free trade area and the common market in order to increase the volume of Canadian trade and raise economic standards in this country.
Something has already been said during this debate as to the United States action in limiting the flow of Canadian oil to that country. The export of Canadian oil to the United States and the development of the eastern Canadian market are most important to the people of western Canada. Recent events in the Middle East might suggest that some of the imports of oil normally coming to Canada from that area may be cut off, and I am wondering if the minister would agree to make a comment as to how any decrease in the flow of oil from Arabia and Iran into Canada would affect the Canadian market for our domestic oil.
The hon. member for Kootenay West in his speech yesterday emphasized the importance of developing the China market. The minister has told us that Canada has increased its trade with China and, in all fairness, this government seems to be interested in developing the market in China. But it seems to me that the government has two policies with regard to China, and that they

are inconsistent policies. The government puts its head in the sand as far as recognizing China is concerned and seems to pretend that the new government of that country does not exist. It tags along with John Foster Dulles and company, refusing to recognize the government of China; but, as if to attempt to gain for Canada the benefits of recognition, the government follows another policy of endeavouring to promote trade.
I am in the main interested in developing the second policy, but I say that if we are to take consistent steps to improve our trade with China then we should recognize the government of that country, and I hope the minister will use his influence within the government to see that such recognition is brought about at an early date. I am certain that such recognition would make easier our relations with China and would of itself lead to a substantial increase in trade with that country.
There is, I believe, one very serious omission from the minister's statement. I could scarcely believe that he had omitted any reference to the growing threat of the U.S.S.R. in the economic field. I do not believe the minister made any reference at all to that matter in his speech. As I read the reports of economists, newspaper writers and, yes, the speeches of heads of states, this would seem to be the major economic development in the world during recent months. There are growing reports that the U.S.S.R. is entering into very serious competition in the field of steel and that United States and Canadian steel prices and production may be seriously affected by such competition from Russia. The Financial Post of June 14, 1958 contained an article headed "Is Russia Gearing Itself for Pulp and Paper Push?", which reads in part as follows:
Foreign observers bring back word from Russia that forest-based industries there are expanding quickly, both in size and efficiency.
For instance there are estimates that Russia is spending $3 billion yearly to hike forest output and efficency.
The minister apparently does not think there is any threat in this regard.
