Growing trade and competition from the Soviet union did not warrant a reference by him at all, yet in the Montreal Gazette of June 5, 1958 there is a report headed "Red Trade 'Grab' Thrust on C.M.A.", which in part reads as follows:
The price war being waged by the Soviet union in its increasing invasion of world export markets, including those for a number of Canadian products, was bluntly thrust upon delegates' attention early in the proceedings.
This cut-price bid for business at the expense of Canada and other western countries was rated by H. V. Lush, of Toronto, C.M.A. president, as "just as dangerous as the military 'cold war' of recent years."
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Those are the words of the president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and the article goes on to say:
Russia, said Mr. Lush, is "pinching our toes" and preparing to "hurt us in the future" with deliberate efforts to "under-cut sensitive markets" at a time of North American economic slowdown.
There seems to be throughout the minister's statement a complete lack of policy and a complete lack of new thinking which the government referred to as being necessary and is thought to be necessary in other countries; and I suggest the only way Canada will be able to increase its share of trade in the world is for the Canadian government itself to take a more active part in promoting such trade.
The one feature of Canadian trade to which the minister was able to refer with pleasure and pride was the increase in Canadian exports of wheat, and this increase was brought about precisely because the government, in this instance, adopted new and far-reaching policies to move a product in surplus supply. The day has now arrived, I suggest, when in terms of trade we need a greater degree of government management and government promotion, and we say again that to deal with the increased threat of Soviet trade the government should be considering the establishment of such a policy, the providing of export and import boards, providing for the sale of Canadian products on a long-term contract basis and also the purchasing of Canadian imports on a long-term contract basis.
The government can pooh-pooh the idea; it can say "this is socialism, we do not have anything to do with it"; but the only product which has shown an increase, namely wheat, is sold by a government board that has complete control over the buying and selling of that product in respect to interprovincial and export trade, and also because the government had adopted new policies to promote the sale of that product.
The day of looking to convertibility of currency, the day when you can expect all the so-called free enterprisers who are engaged in the production and sale of various commodities consistently to expand Canadian trade year after year, is over; and these people and these industries, in the very words of some of their officers and some of their authorities, will not be able to meet the increased competition from the Soviet union which, they have been saying in recent days, is more dangerous to our way of life than the cold war itself.
I suggest that when the minister makes his statement he should give the house concrete proposals which he thinks will result in increasing Canadian trade, and I express the

Supply-Trade and Commerce hope that he can give us some assurance that in the year ahead our exports can increase by a volume very substantially higher than the 2 per cent increase of last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 391 carry?
The minister has been asked a number of questions, and I think it is customary about this time for him to make something of a general reply to the many questions that have been put to him.
I am quite prepared to do so, but the hon. member sat down somewhat more hurriedly than I had expected.
Just two minutes short of my full time.

I appreciate that the house would like to proceed as rapidly as possible with the estimates of this department, recognizing at the same time that in view of the importance of the department there should be no undue haste. But with the summer getting rather warm and the end of the session, perhaps, not too far away, I feel quite certain that hon. members would like to proceed as rapidly as possible with this department so they can deal with the others.
The haste is all on your side.

No, I am quite patient about this. 1 appreciate the attention which has been paid to this subject of trade, and I am grateful for the kind remarks which most of the members participating have made with regard to the efforts the government is making toward increasing trade. I appreciate very much the suggestions which have been made for further improvements, even if I do not accept them all.
The speeches we have heard so far are typical of speeches from the opposition. One of the great advantages of spending several years in the opposition and transferring to the government side is that one knows precisely the type of speech that may emerge from opposition ranks. When I sat over there I used to examine the speeches made by the minister introducing the estimates of whatever department it was, and if I could find no fault with his speech-which is very much what has happened in the course of this debate so far-I would then look for omissions, things which had not been mentioned.
Members of the opposition have assisted me in this respect and pointed out all my sins of omission. And then I would go on to examine very carefully the policy as set out by the minister, or lack of policy, depending upon the point of view. All of that is perfectly right for an opposition, and I understand the attitude of hon. members and think


their contribution to the debate has been constructive.
It will not be possible for me to answer every question that has been asked. If I omit answering something that should be answered I hope hon. members will draw my attention to it, because it will not have been done intentionally. I recall that some years ago when I was then critical of the then minister of national defence on his estimates, he would answer all the other opposition members who had spoken and leave me out entirely, which is not the type of treatment I propose to offer on this occasion. So if I do omit something please draw my attention to it. However, I will try to deal with some of the questions that have been raised, and in view of the contribution made this morning by the Leader of the Opposition perhaps I may begin by making a few comments on that.
I think in his usual fashion, as he got near the end of his speech and began dealing with the realm of external affairs, the hon. gentleman waxed eloquent-he is always more at home in this field than with regard to certain other matters-and drew our attention to what he called a broader vision of a western world more closely tied together economically. He spoke about freer Atlantic trade.
I fully appreciate his views in this regard, and draw his attention to the fact that in the spring of 1952 when I was seated in approximately the place now occupied by the hon. member for St. Boniface, and when my speeches in the House of Commons did not receive the attention which they perhaps deserved, I spoke on the subject of closer union of the Atlantic community and expressed sentiments somewhat similar to those expressed by the Leader of the Opposition today.
That is, I had what he calls a vision of a more closely linked Atlantic community; and in those days-and I hold the same opinion today-I thought it would be wise for us as western democracies to come more closely together than we were at that time, or are at this very moment, if we were to protect ourselves against the growing threat of nations which hold a different view on political matters. Part of that unity can be achieved, just as the Leader of the Opposition said, through closer links by way of trade. To that extent we are together in our thinking.
The hon. member was led into a final discussion of the European common market and the European free trade area, subjects which have been touched upon by the hon. member for Assiniboia and others. May I say that we are well aware of the problems that may arise if the European common market countries erect restrictive barriers against

trade with Canada. But as I pointed out in my speech yesterday, we have received assurances from them that that is not the intention. Moreover, they are all members of GATT and will negotiate with us under the terms of the GATT agreement.
I do not hold the views that some people do with regard to what may happen to our trade if the common market countries proceed with their plans. I think the six nations joining together and having free trade within their borders will lead to a higher standard of living in those countries, which in turn will result in greater buying power; and forecasts made of the six-nation common market development in Europe indicate that there will be an increase in population and an increase in productivity, just as happened on the North American continent, leading to an increase ability to purchase commodities from abroad. Thus it is not with alarm that I view the development of the arrangement among the six nations of Europe. At the same time we are keeping in contact with them in order that Canada's interests may not be overlooked.
The European free trade area is similarly being watched, and we have had adequate assurances from the United Kingdom that agricultural imports from Canada will not suffer any restriction if and when the United Kingdom enters into the free trade area with other nations of Europe. We are well aware of these problems and are keeping closely in contact with them.
Well, it was from a discussion of this that the Leader of the Opposition went on to his rather splendid climax, but earlier he was worrying himself about the co-called United Kingdom offer of free trade with Canada. I asked him to put on record the Liberal party's statement of policy in so far as that was concerned, and I indicated that the concluding phrases or sentences of that policy hedged it about so that it is almost if not entirely meaningless.
Then the Leader of the Opposition elaborated. He said, "Had this offer been made to us when we were in power we would have said, 'we will examine it; we will give sympathetic consideration to it, but we will go a step further, we will say now this is fine for the United Kingdom and for Canada, but let us not forget the United States; let us bring the United States in as well, and then we must not forget the commonwealth, and the commonwealth countries must be considered' ". So this sets the stage a little more broadly and extends the conversation.
Then I suppose he would have carried it a little further and said there are nations outside the commonwealth, not on the North
Supply-Trade and Commerce American continent, that should be brought into this idea of freer trade among the nations. And I am sure that before the deliberations would have gone very far my hon. friend, had he been in office, would have said, in view of the probability of interplanetary communication, perhaps no further steps should be taken until the attitude of the residents of Mars had been considered. That is the way you consider, that is the way you take into account-
That is an excuse for doing nothing.

-the so-called free trade offer from the United Kingdom to Canada.
We are quite prepared to consider any suggestion with regard to expanding trade, but my hon. friend knows that suggestion was put forward as an objective, just as the suggestion of a closer link among the Atlantic community is an objective that can be worked for. It cannot be accomplished overnight and our United Kingdom friends said that this cannot be done in a day, a month or a year, and it might take 12 or 15 years to bring to fruition. Why are my hon. friends so alarmed about this matter? Let them produce some ideas themselves as to what might be done. We do not differ from them in being desirous of expanding trade, lowering the restrictions that now exist with regard to trade, and generally bringing nations closer together through the medium of trade.
Quite a number of references were made to China. I think we should keep the discussion with regard to China in proportion. There is theoretically a very large market there, 600 million people. If they all wanted television sets and refrigerators, why you would be kept busy for the next six generations supplying them. But it just does not follow that you can immediately expand Canada's trade with a country like China. Our policy is to make some attempt along that line, and that is precisely what we have been doing.
Canada's trade with China has been going on for years. It did not just start when we came into office or when our friends were in office; it has been going on for years. Since the war and the revolution in China that trade has been curtailed; nevertheless certain articles have been exchanged between our two countries over the years. During this year we were fortunate to re-establish a trade in wheat with China which 20-odd years ago was substantial. I think we are justified in taking some pride in the fact that several cargoes of wheat have been sold to China. That trade, if it can be maintained and expanded, might very well reach the proportions in the future that it was years

Supply-Trade and Commerce ago, and surplus wheat production in Canada might be utilized in the Far East. Therefore I think we are on the right ground there.
With regard to restrictions on trade with China, the Leader of the Opposition was asking about the strategic list and I think someone else questioned me as to what articles might not be sold to China. I have here a publication issued by the queen's printer, a reprint of the Canada Gazette, part II, volume 91, dated January 9, 1957, when my hon. friends were in office. It is called the Export and Import Permits Act, export control list. It gives the list of materials which are under control, and at the present moment negotiations are going on at the so-called COCON conference to see whether or not the list may be modified, but there is nothing concealed about it. Anyone may have a copy of it if they wish to get it and see what articles are under prohibition.
I noticed that the Leader of the Opposition had something to say with regard to our increased exports, particularly in wheat; and, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia, he tried to make it appear that nothing we had done as a government had brought about the increase in the sale of wheat this year; that it was the short crop in Australia, the smaller crop in the Argentine, the higher protein value of the Canadian wheat, and so on.
These factors have their place in world trade in wheat. On the other hand he might have pointed out that there was a very large surplus of wheat in the United States which has its effect on the Canadian market in international trade, and that there was a very large European crop of wheat, which balanced out any loss in world production in the Argentine or in Australia. Although we cannot take credit for everything that happened with regard to trade in wheat, nevertheless as a government we did take some new measures and showed considerable activity in supporting the wheat board in suggestions they made with regard to increasing our sales of wheat abroad.
My first act after being sworn in on June 21, 1957, was to go out to Winnipeg and meet the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners for two days rather than asking them to come to Ottawa. That was the start of our developing a policy with regard to the sale of our surplus grains. Subsequently I met the wheat board again, journeyed with members of that wheat board to Europe in September, spent 10 days there calling upon and meeting over 200 representatives of the grain trade in Europe and assuring them that Canada would not enter into any sharp pricecutting war and was not going to upset the market in wheat.

Subsequently it was the policy of the government to make available wheat and flour to Pakistan, India and Ceylon under either a long-term loan or an outright gift to the extent of supplying $35 million for loan purposes and $15 million for outright gift purposes. Then for the Palestinian refugees, who have been in desperate straits for many years in the area of the border between Palestine and Egypt, we made an outright gift of $1J million worth of flour.
All this was in addition to and without interfering with the normal development program under the Colombo plan to which a grant of $35 million has been made annually for several years. That was a forward looking policy with regard to the disposal of surplus food, and it was a policy devised and put into operation by this government. It resulted in moving a substantial quantity of wheat from the prairies, and I think the Canadian people as a whole approve of it. The more wheat we move from the prairies and from the elevators, the less we eventually pay for storage and the greater the advantage to the people of the world who require food.
That was the program during last winter. These things taken together made up our policy with regard to wheat and have resulted, when you take all factors into account, in a very good year with regard to the sale of wheat. We will exceed last year's record by 40 million or 50 million bushels, and the record of two years ago of 309 million bushels exported will be exceeded as well.
My only difficulty at the moment is that if we set too high a record in the export of wheat this year we will be under the grave difficulty of matching it a year from now. If we reach 320 million bushels this year the hon. member for Assiniboia, who wants our export of wheat now to be 350 million bushels, will raise that figure to 380 million. I am always at a disadvantage with my hon. friend who likes to be just one jump ahead of whatever anyone else proposes or whatever is being done. That is the record of the government and the wheat board with regard to our wheat sales, and it has all resulted not from an aggressive sales program as some people have called it-I have never used that term-but from an active policy directed toward moving our wheat into international trade.
I was very grateful to the Leader of the Opposition for drawing my attention to a word in the annual report of the department which, of course, I had not seen before and was not aware of. He referred to the sentence in the report of a year ago, "Various reports were prepared for official use", and pointed out that in the report this year the word

"mainly" had crept in so the sentence read, "Various reports were prepared mainly for official use."
It crept in?

I know how it got there, but I am not going to make any accusations. Of course I did not see the report until it was in published form and I did not compare it with that of the previous year. The burden the Leader of the Opposition has now placed on deputy ministers is that they will have to produce the preceding year's report and indicate to the minister the changes from the normal sentences which will appear in the new report, so it is an added burden on the civil service in the future. I am very grateful to the Leader of the Opposition for drawing my attention to that.
In well run departments it was always done that way.

Sometimes these reports are published during the course of an election campaign when it is not possible to see everything that is coming out. There has been some talk about uranium. Exports of uranium certainly have added to our total export position this year, and we are very grateful that the world needs uranium and that Canada has the supplies. As a matter of fact uranium exports for the first five months of this year reached a total of $89.9 million compared with $35.7 million the year before, and we expect that these exports will continue to add greatly to our export position certainly for several more years. It is rather difficult to see too far ahead but we are blessed with a bountiful supply of uranium and it may well be that as atomic energy is put to use more widely throughout the world, even after 1962 there will be an enlarged demand for uranium. Canada will be in a position to supply the world with the uranium that will be required for the various power plants that are now beginning to appear in different countries in the world.
I make no excuses for presenting the picture of our external trade in the best light. I have not intentionally concealed any facts. I pointed out in my speech that it is due to greater sales of wheat, uranium and cattle that the picture looks as favourable as it does at the present moment. There were reductions in the sales of other commodities. I did not list them in the course of my speech, but I mentioned the fact that there were reductions here and there.
The hon. member for Assiniboia thinks I was very complacent with regard to the trade picture. I had no intention of indicating any complacency, but I think it is a matter of pride for Canada that with a recession
Supply-Trade and Commerce prevailing on the North American continent, we nevertheless had a larger export trade than a year ago. My hon. friend wants our export trade to be higher than it is at the moment, but he takes that position on everything that comes before the house. If I had said that our export position was 5 per cent or 10 per cent greater than a year ago he would have said that it should have been 20, 25 or 30 per cent greater. Once again it is impossible to satisfy that type of criticism of the facts of the case.
Would the minister permit a question?
There is no complacency at all.
Is the minister satisfied with the 1 per cent increase in the first few months of this year over last year?

I would have been terribly disturbed if the figure had been 1 per cent below the exports of last year, but we are holding our own and are doing better than some other countries. This is partly due to the policy of the government, the activity of the trade commissioners representing us throughout the world, and the excellent work being done by Canadian businessmen who are pushing their products in so many countries of the world. I think full credit should go to them for maintaining our exports at their present high level.
I used to be very good at listing omissions in speeches in days gone by, and my hon. friends opposite are doing quite well at it. The list of omissions includes one mentioned by both the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia. They said I had paid no attention in my speech to the growing threat of the economic warfare being conducted by the U.S.S.R. I could have included everything in my speech if I had continued for two hours. Many years ago speeches in the house used to run from two to five and a half or seven hours, but the modern practice has been to reduce the length of speeches.
So there were omissions; but the only reason I omitted a reference to that economic threat was that it had been mentioned so frequently either in the house in answer to questions or in public statements made by the Prime Minister in addresses elsewhere in the country. It was only a few days ago that the Prime Minister, speaking on the occasion of the visit of the President of the United States, and the President himself, made reference to this situation. On page
2386	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce 2801 of Hansard for July 9, 1958 we find the words of the Prime Minister of Canada:
The communist world is waging an intensive economic global offensive of "aid and trade", an offensive which is not designed to secure profits in a bookkeeping sense in order to secure the ordinary values of trade for its peoples, but an offensive whose success will be measured by the degree to which the souls and hearts and the freedoms and aspirations of the recipients will be subverted under communist tyranny.
On other occasions he has mentioned this economic warfare, and in his statement the President mentioned it as well. I thought it was well understood by all hon. members, and that everybody in Canada was aware of that threat. We are well aware of it. There is the threat with regard to aluminum. We have looked into that. We have made representations to the United Kingdom, one of the great buyers of our aluminum, asking them to continue to purchase the Canadian product despite offers that might be made by the Russians at a much lower figure. We are fully conscious of the threat posed by the economic warfare of communist countries.
I received some advice and some comments, Mr. Chairman, from the member for Ottawa West yesterday with regard to which I might make some answer. Apparently I have dealt with quite a number of the things he brought to my attention. He did deal at some length with our trade with the West Indies and thought I had not made any elaboration of our policy with regard to those countries. That is quite right; I did not elaborate-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order; I must advise the Minister of Trade and Commerce that his time has expired.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Has the minister unanimous consent to continue
Agreed.

I held out the suggestion of a 5-hour speech, and I think hon. members have agreed to that. I did not elaborate with regard to the West Indies for this reason. They are in the process of forming their federation. They have to effect a customs union amongst the islands that make up the federation before they will be in a position to deal on a government to government basis with other countries with regard to general trade matters. We have a sympathetic interest in the West Indies. We want to promote our trade with those islands, and our trade is complementary. We have the industrial base here and the manufactured goods to exchange with them for the tropical products which they can produce. Our trade with the West Indies has been going on for several generations, and I think can be extended.


Of course the hon. member for Ottawa West used this topic as a club to belabour me with regard to the decrease in shipping lines to the West Indies. This is not an immediate problem of mine, and he perhaps should save his remarks for some other occasion. On the other hand we have gone this far, that we have offered to construct and give to the West Indies a ship for their interisland trade capable of travelling from Jamaica to Trinidad, a distance of something over 1,000 miles. There are ships from Canada engaged in the West Indies, though certain boats have been withdrawn from that trade. There is no evidence that the general trade with the West Indies has been seriously curtailed on that account.
I should like to mention two very helpful speeches which were made yesterday by representatives from Newfoundland, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. They gave some very helpful suggestions with regard to the fisheries industry in Newfoundland. I have read the speeches over again because of my interest in the subject. As I think I have mentioned, we have had six conferences with representatives from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia on the subject of Atlantic fisheries, and the speeches of my hon. friends have added some information to that supplied by those who have visited here.
I confess that like my hon. friend the member for Bonavista-Twillingate, coming as we both do from Manitoba, neither of us was as knowledgable with regard to the fishing industry of Newfoundland as we are becoming. My hon. friend, of course, has a greater knowledge of it than I have because he has a constituency there to represent. I note a similarity between the problems of the fishermen in the Atlantic coastal regions and the prairie farmers. There may be a need to take some new and different action with regard to the fisheries problems on the Atlantic coast. What that action should be I cannot say at the moment, but I am open to suggestions from hon. members who have had vast experience with regard to the Atlantic fisheries.
The government can only play a certain part with regard to the export of fish from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. There are other voluntary organizations playing a part in that situation. With regard to Brazil, Jamaica and the other countries that are consumers of Canadian fish, naturally the government can make representations and endeavour through trade agreements or other means to maintain our markets there. The government cannot take some steps which appear to me to be necessary-and these were

not mentioned by my hon. friends-perhaps to raise the quality of the product that is now being marketed.
I recall some conversations with representatives of the fishing industry in the Atlantic region-I hope someone will correct me if I am not right in this statement-and I understand that we are not producing the types of graded fish that some of our customers would like to have. Whether or not my colleague the Minister of Fisheries will be able to produce some solution to that I do not know. But from the standpoint of the Department of Trade and Commerce we are doing what we can to stimulate the sale of fish from the Atlantic coast.
I think I can safely assure my hon. friends that our market in Jamaica has just been lost temporarily. The information I have had is that we will be back into that market. I hope that as we continue our negotiations, and as the Federation of the West Indies is more fully developed, we will establish very firmly our trade in fish with the West Indies so we will not run the hazard again of being undersold by subsidized fish products from other countries.
Other members made suggestions of one sort or another which perhaps we could take up as we come to the various items that are scattered through the estimates.
I presume I could go on at some length just in a debating sense countering arguments that were raised. On the other hand, it might be better if we got down to the specific items. If I have omitted things that I should have commented on, I will gladly take them up. I have not mentioned the contribution made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres except jocularly last night, the hon. member for Cartier and the hon. member for Mount Royal. We heard from the hon. member for Kootenay West, the hon. member for Timis-kaming, the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Port Arthur. I was grateful to the hon. member for Vancouver South for his comments on our trade with China and to the hon. member for Rosthern for his suggestions.
I think the hon. member for Macleod put his finger on the trouble that affects trade, wherein we fail sometimes to analyse the picture accurately and determine the dollar exchange balance because, as he pointed out, there can be no effective trade with another country unless they have dollars with which to buy our products. Basically that is one of the problems affecting world trade. The whole question of the price of primary products throughout the world is one which is before the nations now for consideration and I hope it will be considered at the commonwealth conference. If the price of primary
Supply-Trade and Commerce products is depressed, the countries producing those primary products cannot earn the dollars necessary to buy the manufactured articles that they require.
One of the reasons for our emphasis on trade throughout the world is that we may, by buying or in some way getting imports from abroad, make it possible for those countries in their turn to take the products that we have for sale such as our forest products, the products of our mines and our agricultural products. If they have not earned the dollars, how can they purchase our products? That is why we want to diversify our trade and buy many things from other countries of the world. If we buy from the West Indies bauxite and alumina, citrus fruits and so on they will buy our fish. If we buy from the United Kingdom in quantity, we can sustain our market there for 100 million bushels of wheat each year. These aspects of our trade are constantly in our mind. That is why we want to broaden it out so that it is not too greatly concentrated in any one place.
That, Mr. Chairman, constitutes my reply to those who have spoken thus far. I hope that I shall be able to give answers to any who feel that they have been overlooked in the interval.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wonder whether I could
ask the minister a question. I do not -want to hold up this item. He has dealt with the subject matter of trade and commerce at some length. But from time to time during the question period last session and, I believe, once during the question period this session I asked him whether he could tell the house what had been the result in dollars or pounds sterling of the trade mission to the United Kingdom and what amount of trade had been thus diverted? I remember that at one time he or someone announced that the hydro electric power commission of Ontario had given a large order for the purchase of electrical equipment for the main powerhouse at Cornwall. I believe there was also some question of the purchase of tin-plate by certain manufacturers in this country. I think the gist of the minister's answer from time to time was that in due course it would be possible for him to give a reply to the house as to the amount of purchases in dollars or pounds sterling. I wondered whether this could be done at this time.

There has been considerable interest in the trade mission that visited England last fall and a certain amount of understandable curiosity on the part of my hon. friends opposite as to the exact dollars and cents return from that mission. I may at some time have said that in due course I would be able to provide the figures for

Supply-Trade and Commerce which my hon. friend is now asking. I have not those figures here today. I do not think they can be obtained very readily. I always considered that, as the months went by, the effect of that trade mission would become clearly evident. It is not a question of deciding this week or this month what purchases were made in the United Kingdom as a direct result of the trade mission. The only way in which I could get that information would be from members of the trade mission reporting directly to me as to the purchases which they made and which on other occasions they might have made elsewhere. Two or three members of the trade mission have indicated to me that they were considering very large orders with the United Kingdom as a result of their visit there.
It is all a matter of private business, and until these orders are placed and the goods are shipped it would be just impossible to get an answer that would satisfy my hon. friend. Perhaps later on towards the end of this year, as companies compile their returns and as the bureau of statistics reports on imports from abroad, we might be able to segregate some of these items and determine that these were directly the result of that trade mission. I am positive that we are getting results from that trade mission because of the statements that members of that mission have made to me, from the inquiries that have come from British industry, from the visit of British industrialists here some time ago. There is more to it than just the purchase of some goods from England at this particular moment. We look to see the establishment in this country of more branch plants from England. We are looking forward to a larger capital investment on the part of the people of the United Kingdom. We are looking forward to an increase in our imports from the United Kingdom with respect to goods that are not now manufactured in Canada. Those are, broadly, the purposes of that mission; and so far I have had no evidence that those purposes are not being fulfilled.
While I am on that topic may I say that someone was asking-it was the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres-about component parts of articles shipped into this country from the United States, and he thought that I gave a rather abrupt answer last winter, something which was not intended. I will give him a better answer now, or at least I hope it is a better answer. In the case of imports of manufactured goods from the United States such as tractors, these imports are attributed to the United States where the finished article is fabricated or assembled and subsequently consigned to


Canada. Likewise imports of textiles manufactured in the United Kingdom are attributed to the United Kingdom even though the materials from which the textiles are made may originate in the United States or some other country. Canadian exports-for example automobiles-may contain materials or components which have originated in the United States or other countries but to trace the ultimate origin of materials or components of commodities imported or exported would be a formidable task involving extensive and expensive investigation. The information required is not now available to the government and would have to be sought from the business firms involved in particular trading transactions not only in Canada but also abroad.
That just indicates the difficulty in answering what is, I am prepared to admit, a question which arises in the minds of many people. In fact, the six nation common market group over in Europe are taking into consideration a problem allied to this one as to imports where the country of origin may have to be shown. However, in so far as we are concerned, no statistics are compiled and it is very very difficult to give the hon. member a better answer than I have done.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I thank the minister for the time he has taken to deal with my question. It is a most incomplete answer; but as he says, it takes some time in order to ascertain what the effects of a trade mission of this nature would be. I would draw his attention to the fact, however, that when I asked my question it was over ten months ago and I have received no answer but I will still be willing to wait patiently in the hope that at a later date there will be some positive results to be reported.
It seems to me that when the mission departed it was in conjunction with the proposed diversion of 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom -that seemed to be the objective of the trade mission-and the other question I would like to ask the minister is, has the idea of diverting that 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom now been abandoned?
I have never understood that any policy was announced framed in the terms of a 15 per cent diversion of trade from the United States to the United Kingdom.
Oh, Oh.
I said policy-
Was it a vision?
I have always understood that the phrase was used as an indication of what would happen-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I used the word objective.

As an objective. The objective of the mission to the United Kingdom was not based on any percentage. Our objective was definitely based on obtaining from the United Kingdom materials and supplies which are now coming from foreign countries and which are not now obtainable or manufactured in Canada and it was part of a program to reestablish a better balance in our trading relations.
I pointed out in my speech yesterday that our trade with the United States of America was of paramount importance-it has been so for generations and will continue to be so- but on the other hand over the last 15 years we have felt that that trade has got out of balance. We are buying from the United States over $1 billion more each year than we sell to them. We are not asking them to balance our trade out to the last degree but if they would take more of our products we would not be under this disability. We do, of course, produce things which the United States does not require-for example, Canadian wheat. There is no market for Canadian wheat in the United States and so we have to sell it to the United Kingdom, the European markets, Japan, China, Africa and so on, and our flour made from Canadian wheat goes around the world. The United States does not require flour at all. As I said earlier, the countries which do require and might use Canadian wheat and flour have to have the purchasing dollars to buy those products; they have to have something to exchange with us and so we have to trade with nations throughout the world.
If our trade is funnelled into one channel, namely the United States, how do we make it possible for these other countries to trade with us? We simply say it is wiser and safer to have our trade spread out among many countries and with respect to the $1 billion which we spend as an excess figure in relation to our imports from the United States each year, some of that money might be spent in Europe or in Japan or in Africa or in Latin America to buy products from those countries. They in their turn would buy manufactured goods from Canada or Canadian wheat or Canadian lumber.
That is the situation. Fifteen years ago Britain's share in the Canadian market was much higher than it is today and we suggested to them that here was an opportunity for them to re-establish their position in Canada's import market and get back to what was considered years ago to be a good
Supply-Trade and Commerce pattern of trade-the triangular trade of Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States. The United Kingdom industrial component is now in such a condition, having recovered from the war, that it can produce many of the things Canada now gets from the United States and does not herself manufacture, indeed, which we might more wisely buy from the United Kingdom.
That is our policy. The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Ottawa West were today lamenting the fact that our imports had declined; they said nothing about the fact that some of those articles formerly imported are now being manufactured in Canada. It is not dire ruin if your import figure goes down if, at the same time, your manufacturing figure goes up. Last year we imported less pipe for pipe lines than we would have done because of the fact that in Canada we can now produce the type of pipe in the size and quality desired. With respect to the pipe lines across this country, compressor stations are required to boost up the pressure, forcing the gas or oil along the line, and during the past 12 months a Canadian firm has been able to manufacture and supply compressors for one of those lines. This has reduced the import figure from the United States because those compressors would have come from that country had they not been manufactured here. So although we are trying to get our general trading pattern into better balance, we are not overlooking the fact that those who want to speak in terms of diversion of trade might get equal results by stimulating manufacturing in Canada, thereby reducing imports from the United States.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the minister has mentioned one or two points with which I had attempted to deal, and in order to make sure there will be no misunderstanding with respect to what I said or intended to say, I wish to state that I was not opposed to a decrease in the amount of imports into this country if this was done as a result of the replacement of those imports by Canadian goods manufactured at reasonable cost and on an economic basis. Of course that is all to the good and such a diminution of imports is helpful. Furthermore, when we can diminish our imports by diversion-I am not afraid to use the word-to countries which have need of dollars to purchase Canadian goods and where we can get similar materials from those countries at a reasonable and competitive price, this is also desirable.
The main reasons, however, for the diminution of imports from the United States in recent months have not, surely, been the

Supply-Trade and Commerce increase of Canadian production, although that no doubt has had some effect, nor has it been because these imports have been diverted to the United Kingdom. Imports have diminished from the United States because of the fact that our investment situation and our trading picture in this country-are such that we did not need to import capital goods such as we required a few years ago for our great development program. That surely is the major reason why imports have gone down. It is not the only reason but it must be the major one. When the minister talks about the desirability of restoring the pattern of trade to that of the old days-the triangular pattern-we must of course all agree with him. He must, however, know that no country and no government could have done much more to restore that pattern than the Canadian government has done since 1945.
That pattern cannot be restored until the pound is made convertible. You cannot have a triangular pattern of the old kind without convertibility of the pound, and when the British were unable to make the pound convertible after world war II because of the financial circumstances at that time arising out of the sacrifices they had made, the Canadian government made a great many dollars available to them-$2 billion-to help them get in a position where they could make the pound convertible and restore the triangular pattern of trade which was previously our salvation, if that is not too strong a word, and which we all hope will be restored before long. But this is something which the government of the United Kingdom has to decide. I hope the government of Canada, and the minister, will do their best at the forthcoming commonwealth economic conference to see that every possible progress is made in this direction.

That is one of our objectives. I hope I did not give the wrong impression when I was speaking about the question of imports. I did not want to misinterpret the Leader of the Opposition in any way. I was just pointing out one of the omissions in his speech.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have just one other question to ask if I may. The minister in his remarks did not deal at any length with the commonwealth conference to be held at Montreal in September. He made some reference to it in a general way, but I am wondering if he could not go a little further and give us an indication of the subjects likely to come up for discussion. After all, the conference is to take place in barely two months time and there must be a great deal of preparation going on in his department as well as in


other departments which are concerned with it. Perhaps the minister could tell us whether or not the British trade proposals are likely to be considered, and I think the committee would appreciate any other information he might care to give at this time.

I did not deal with this matter at any length because my recollection is that in the budget speech my colleague the Minister of Finance devoted some time to the question of the trade and economic conference which is to be held in September and, in fact, on page 1239 of Hansard I find his reference to that conference occupies virtually an entire page in both English and French in dealing with this. I have no elaboration to offer at the moment.

I think the minister made some reference to the possibility of Canadian subsidiaries of United States firms trading with China. I believe the question of the 1,000 automobile offer to purchase was first disclosed in February or March, but certainly it was long before the federal election, and at that time a statement was made that a thorough investigation would be carried out with regard to this particular offer and especially with regard to the alleged impossibility of Canadian automobile manufacturers supplying these automobiles. We all know that this question was further discussed when President Eisenhower was in Ottawa, and I wonder if the minister could give us some idea of the steps that were taken to make it a thorough inquiry, just what the inquiry involved, and whether he now feels with certainty that any such offers in the future could be accepted and filled by any Canadian company provided it could produce the product at a competitive price. I wonder, now, whether Canadian grain companies which are subsidiaries of United States companies are completely free to develop Chinese markets.
When this question has been raised before in this house the minister has maintained that while a certain number of companies may not be able to undertake this business we were fortunate that there were distinctively Canadian companies which were quite prepared to develop this market and which had been successful to some extent. My question now is: is it completely clear that all grain companies in Canada are free to develop the Chinese market, and is the minister completely confident-I am not sure that this was in his statement-that it is the intention of the United States administration to allow Canadian firms to compete in the nonstrategic field in the Chinese market or in the markets of other communist nations.

I have no evidence to indicate that there was a firm offer and acceptance in regard to the alleged intended purchase of 1,000 automobiles some time ago. However, instances have been brought to my attention of trading deals with China which might have been impeded by the restrictive law of the United States. As the hon. member has mentioned, we did discuss this problem with Mr. Dulles when he was here a few days ago. We received an assurance that the matter would be taken under consideration and we are pursuing the matter further. Although I cannot answer the hon. member's question definitely at this particular moment, I have every confidence that the way is going to be cleared so that we shall not be faced with this problem in the future. That, I hope, will free the hands, if they are tied, of any flour mill operating in this country whose parent is in the United States. But only a few days have elapsed since we had this conversation, and we have not had time to tidy the matter up. However, I have no reason to doubt that we will reach a satisfactory solution.

I was under the distinct impression from the statement the Prime Minister made following the president's visit that it had been tidied up. I am not endeavouring to misinterpret what the Prime Minister said; in thinking he said that, I was apparently in error. Since the matter has not been tidied up and since this process is still going on, can the minister say when he hopes to be in a position to give the Canadian people an unqualified assurance that in the field of nonstrategic goods companies operating within the Canadian borders will be free to take any business that is not barred by Canadian law.

The hon. member asks me to give an assurance when this may happen, or if I am hopeful that this may happen. I live in daily hope that all my problems will be solved within 24 hours. It does not work out that way, but I do have hopes that this particular problem will be solved very shortly.

I should like to follow this up, because the secretary of commerce of the United States is reported to have stated in Washington while the president was visiting this country that exemption from this particular United States law, which has extraterritorial effect, in that it applies to United States citizens and United States corporations and subsidiaries of the United States corporations outside the United States, can be granted by administrative action on the part, presumably, of the president or some member of the executive. He gave the impression in his
Supply-Trade and Commerce statement, as reported from Washington, that that would be done.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if it were a matter of amending the law, that would be a very complicated question indeed and I can understand why the president, or indeed any other member of the administration, could not give the Canadian government the assurances which they might have requested, though this matter has been before the United States government presumably for a good many months. But if it is a matter of administrative action to exempt a corporation, or a person, from the operation of a law, then surely there is no reason why there should not be a statement from the administration in Washington confirming what the secretary of commerce is reported to have said to the effect that when this law operates to interfere with business from Canada of a kind which is proper and legal under Canadian law, that administrative action exempting the Canadian subsidiary from the law will be taken. Surely, the government could press the United States government to give the assurance that that administrative action would be taken in every suitable Canadian case, and then the problem would have been disposed of.

Mr. Chairman, the matter is being actively pursued. If it can be done in the way the Leader of the Opposition suggests, by administrative action, that will be the easy way out. I saw a very brief report along the lines that he mentioned but I have not had any confirmation of it.

I am rather disappointed that we have this kind of explanation now, in the light of the Prime Minister's former statement, because I was under the distinct impression from his statement that the matter had been cleared up at that time to Canada's satisfaction, in that Canada expected that from the moment President Eisenhower made his statement it was being cleared up from that time on and Canadian companies were free to undertake this kind of business.
There is some doubt as to whether a company can or cannot undertake that business because it seems to be waiting on some future action. The minister said it might happen in 24 hours. Now it depends on some future action by the United States administration.

I think what is required is a specific instance where there has been an offer made and they are on the point of acceptance. Then we shall know the actual facts of the case and what may happen. My hon. friend is expecting a little too much too quickly but we are not inactive in this matter. As the Leader of the Opposition understands from his long experience, you have to move

Supply-Trade and Commerce along certain channels and make certain representations. You have to get all the i's dotted and the t's crossed. Governments do not just make those blanket statements without very careful consideration. Therefore, if my hon. friend will be patient I think this will turn out all right. We could not have done more than what has been done at the present time. We made the representations to the people who have the authority to act.
When?
When our distinguished visitors were here. Now it is just a matter of following the thing up.

Mr. Chairman, we on this side really have been pretty patient in this matter. On March 27 I think the Prime Minister said that this question would be taken up immediately with the United States, and he gave the country every reason to believe that not only was it to be taken up but that action would be secured and that United States policy was an infringement of Canadian sovereignty. When we asked the Prime Minister questions in the house a couple of weeks ago as to what action had been taken the minister will remember that he informed us that representations had been made to the United States some time in July, I think it was early in July. But on further examination, the representations turned out to be not governmental, not even diplomatic representations but that an official of his department went over to the United States embassy and talked over the matter with somebody in the embassy, perhaps with the commercial consul.
That is the way you used to do it.
No, that is not the way we used to do it.
That is the way you used to start.
I hope in our day we never waited two months before we made that kind of start.
After the Prime Minister had promised action.

After all this promised action two months ago we had this rather niggling initiative and then the President came. I agree that when the government had the President here they could take it up with him, and that was probably the right procedure to follow then. But it would have been much better if this arrangement had been made through diplomatic discussions before the President got here so that he would have known all about the problem, he would have

been briefed, Mr. Dulles would have been briefed, and all they would have had to do- and this is what you really should do at a summit conference-would be to sign on the dotted line. It would have all been worked out before.
Now, we do not know really what has been worked out, whether the agreement had been merely to consult in the appropriate instances. Whether action can be taken by administrative action. If the latter, as the secretary of commerce of the United States has indicated, I hope the minister will not wait until a concrete case comes up but that he will press the United States government to make a formal statement to the effect that in every such case, if it can be done by administrative action, Canadian corporations will be exempted from the operation of this law, which is the only thing that really we can expect as vindication of our sovereign rights in regard to the control of our exports.

My hon. friend understands that we can ask the administration of any country to do certain things but then action itself rests in their hands.
On the subject of impatience to get an answer to this particular problem, may I point out that the United States law and the regulations governing the authority of United States subsidiaries in a foreign country have been on the statute books of the United States for many years during the period in which my hon. friends were in office here, and the alleged purchase of the 1,000 motor cars from Windsor occurred before my hon. friends were retired from office and they did nothing about it. We were the ones who were impatiently waiting for action from a government that had been in office 22 years.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps my hon. friend will tell me the date on which the law in question was passed in Washington.
Certainly before June 10, 1957.

Indeed it was, Mr. Chairman, but not very long before June 10, 1957, and on no occasion while we were in power was that law in any way, shape or form used against any Canadian exporter to any country of the world and we had no reason to complain at all.

The minister said we cannot do anything concerning a matter within the sovereignty of another country. Surely, the conduct of business organizations within Canada is something which should be within the sovereignty of this nation and of this parliament. If the United States refuses to grant this very fair request, the minister

and the government should consider what I suggested they do a few days ago, namely introduce in parliament a Canadian law requiring Canadian corporations to act in a business way to the advantage of this country and to make it a penalty for them to carry out the law of another foreign country if such a law is detrimental to our nation. I think the statement of the minister that they are still working on the case and we cannot expect to hurry too much is a most disappointing answer.
There seems to have been a great change in the tempo of the government since March 31. Before that time, if something had to be done, it was done forthwith, action was taken quickly. Four months have gone by now and for all we know it may take another four months before the people of this country can be given the full assurance that the welfare of Canada in the selling of its commodities is not to be interfered with by another country.
In his response to a statement that the U.S.S.R. was continuing an all-out trade effort, the minister referred to increased competition from that nation in the field of aluminum. Can he say whether the new, dynamic trade policy of the U.S.S.R. has interfered in any way with the volume of export and conditions of sale of any other Canadian commodities?
I missed one or two words there.

The minister said it was quite apparent that the U.S.S.R. had been very aggressive in the sale of aluminum to European nations and had been cutting prices. Are there other commodities with regard to which we see the effect of this new, aggressive trade policy and, if so, what are the other commodities that are affected? As the minister has said, the Prime Minister has pointed out the very serious aspects for the western world of this new trade policy and trade drive. My general question is: How is it affecting Canada?

Before the minister answers, if the hon. member would permit me I should like to clear up one factual point with regard to what was being discussed before. Did I understand the minister correctly to say that this incident about the 1,000 cars arose when the previous administration was in office? The minister nods indicating that is so. In that case, the minister admits this took place before June 21,
1957,	and that the Prime Minister did nothing whatever about it until March 27,
1958,	four days before the election, at which time he only talked about it. Then it took
57071-3-151
Supply-Trade and Commerce two more months before any action whatsoever was taken and then by a civil servant going down to the embassy here in Ottawa.
Let us get the record straight.
That is what I was trying to do.
My hon. friend is very ingenious-
I was reciting the facts.
-at establishing records. My information is that the alleged transaction was initiated when my hon. friends were in office. It did not come to our attention until just before the election in 1958.
Does the minister know whether it was ever brought to the attention of anybody in Ottawa before March 27, 1958?
I always assumed that you people knew everything down here.
Is the minister going to answer my question?

I am sorry. I do not have information available as to specific items in which Canada's trade has been interfered with seriously. I have mentioned aluminum with regard to which I have some accurate knowledge. I believe that our lumber exports have suffered quite a bit from Russian competition.

What about wheat? I know that eastern countries have been buying some wheat from us. I refer specifically to the increase of 34 million acres in wheat production that it is said the Soviet union has accomplished in the last two or three years. Has the minister any comments to make on whether there is any appearance of increased competition from the U.S.S.R. in this field at this time and whether the production from this new 34 million acres, which is one and half times the acreage of Canadian wheat production, is likely to be serious?

I was not aware of that very large increase in the acreage devoted to wheat in Russia but from time to time Russia has had wheat for export. We have never been sure whether this was due to a surplus quantity of wheat or whether it was being exported for some other reason. As my hon. friend knows from his experience as a farmer, crop conditions vary from year to year and although increased acreage may pose a threat weather conditions can remove it.

The minister must have seen press reports in the last three or four years, as all of us have, to the effect that Russia was endeavouring, if I remember correctly, to bring about 70 million new acres of virgin

Supply-Trade and Commerce land into the production of grain crops, most of it in Siberia. While I think reports will show that they have not reached that goal, I do think the report of 34 million acres additional land in grain production in this morning's press is very likely to be correct. It would seem to me that Canada should at all times be studying the situation and be aware of any great drive to increase grain production in a country like the Soviet union because the new drive in the export field that country is now undertaking may have very serious consequences for the Canadian agricultural industry. I hope it will not and I do not know that it is now but it would seem to me that this is part and parcel of the Soviet union's economic drive to step up the production of aluminum, steel, pulp and now wheat.
May I ask the hon. member whether he is sure about the figure of 34 million acres?

That is why I am asking the minister. It would seem to me that with the many trade commissioners and embassy and other officials and his intimate knowledge himself he is the man to give us the correct figures. I was merely saying that on the basis of press reports I have seen over a number of years and in the absence of any statement by the minister to the contrary it would seem to me that the figure of 34 million acres might well prove to be correct.

I am not sure that it is possible to get information with regard to matters in Russia that is completely accurate or satisfying. I think there has always been some difficulty along that line. However, we do attempt to keep informed with regard to wheat production throughout the world and we do not look with too great favour on countries which are subsidizing the production of wheat on a high cost basis when we have here in Canada the best wheat producing land in the world and can produce wheat at a lower cost than almost any other country. Were it not for the long freight haul we would foe in an even better position competitively. But I do not think we need to become too alarmed with regard to an unknown number of acres put into wheat in Russia. Suppose this has happened. Suppose that an additional 34 million acres of wheat are grown in Russia and a tremendous surplus of wheat becomes available in that country. I presume at that stage my hon. friend will ask what the policy of the Canadian government is, but I would prefer to wait and see before we are pushed into that position.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to revert to another matter discussed earlier having to do with trade with the West Indies. The minister said earlier that that was not an immediate problem of his.
No, the ships.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I agree that from an administrative standpoint it is not. The ships are owned by Canadian National Steamships and the person who speaks on their behalf in the House of Commons is the Minister of Transport. But I am sure that in the over-all aspect and having in mind the field of trade the minister considers and realizes that it is a matter of deep concern to his department. I raise the problem because, as the minister knows, one of his predecessors in office, the late Hon. Mr. MacKinnon, spent a great deal of time in activating trade between Canada and the West Indies. Indeed, he made several trips and I think he had a lot to do with enhancing the atmosphere of friendship that already existed between Canada and the various islands of the West Indies.
The problem that arises and gives me some concern, notwithstanding what the minister has said, is that the government has stood by while these eight ships were being withdrawn from service. He said here that he did not consider the trade between the islands and Canada had been seriously curtailed because of this withdrawal. Of course, I cannot challenge that statement other than to say I doubt very much the accuracy of it. After all, there was a considerable amount of trade carried by these eight vessels. The fact a new ship is going to be furnished by the federal government is not going to have any effect at all on the trade because that ship is going to operate between the various islands of the West Indies. It will, I am sure, create good will for Canada, but it is not going to help the actual trade between Canada and the West Indies.
The question I am prompted to ask now is this. Does the minister not think that a serious attempt ought to have been made by the government to keep these ships in operation? Failing that, if a sale has to be made as seems to have been the decision now, would it not have been better to sell them to some agency in the West Indies in order to maintain the trade between the two countries?

As the hon. member was asking these questions my mind went back a few years and I found myself regretting that I had not paid more attention to the Department of Transport when I was in the opposition instead of paying so much attention to the Department of National Defence.

Then I would have been able to put to the then minister some of the difficult questions which he is now putting to me. In those days I directed my attention to other departments. I did not want to get involved in a discussion of the ships that my hon. friend has mentioned, because I thought this was a topic he would prefer to discuss with the Minister of Transport.
With regard to whether or not our trade with the West Indies has been curtailed, the hon. member says my statement may not be correct. That question was asked in the house some time ago and the information I received at that time was that other shipping interests had taken up the trade formerly carried by these Canadian National vessels. Whether or not the information I received was accurate, at any rate I was informed there had been no curtailment of trade between Canada and the West Indies. I am quite prepared to have another look at it, and if it develops that the trade between our countries has been adversely affected by the discontinuance of this particular line of ships, then of course we might have to review the matter. But I have no knowledge at the moment that any of the trade between Canada and the West Indies is less today than it was earlier because these ships are no longer in service.

Some time ago the Minister of Fisheries, and I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce, held a meeting with representatives of the Newfoundland salt fish trade association, the Newfoundland department of fisheries, the Newfoundland federation of fishermen, and representatives of the Nova Scotia salt fish exporters association to study the many and varied problems of the salt fish industry. I should be grateful if the minister would advise this house if he is prepared to make a statement on the outcome of this meeting.

I believe I made a statement with regard to meeting these various organizations the other day in answer to a question in the house. My hon. friend is now asking, what was the outcome of this meeting. This meeting was very informative. I am very grateful to the people who came to Ottawa to give us the information that they had. These men had years of experience, either as fishermen themselves or in endeavouring to sell the products of the fisheries. Quite a number of suggestions were put forward with a view to the improvement of the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast.
The decision I came to, after listening to these representations along with my colleagues the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of National Revenue, was that on
57071-3-151J
Supply-Trade and Commerce the official level discussions should continue, and plans would be formulated, if at all possible, aimed at improving the fishing industry of the Atlantic provinces along the lines suggested by those people who came to see us. Some of the things they mentioned had to do with the processing of the fish; the packaging of the fish; methods of shipping or warehousing; overseas shipments; general sales promotion; things of that nature. The officials have been instructed to continue negotiations and evolve a plan, and to put that plan before us as soon as that can be conveniently done.
I was impressed by the fact that the fishing industry does require something in the nature of assistance, whether it is through advice as to how best it should operate or the assistance of departmental officials in organizational plans, something along that line, I do not know. Apparently something has to be done to assist the fishing industry of the Atlantic coast. Whether the plan evolved will come from those actively engaged in fishing, from the Newfoundland provincial government, from the Department of Trade and Commerce, from the Department of Fisheries or from a combination of all four, I am not sure. However, this combination of four has been instructed to get to work to see if some plan cannot be formulated.

I should like to follow that up for a moment, if I may. I do not want to press the minister about what he said about Jamaica. I was very much encouraged by his confident expression that we would be back in the Jamaican salt fish market at the end of this six-month period. I hope his optimism is well founded. I realize it might be awkward to pursue this matter at this time when negotiations are presumably taking place.
I should like, however, to be assured by the minister that active steps are being taken, rather more active steps than seem to have been taken about this motor car trade with China, to get back into the Brazilian market. At one time this was a very big market and it was lost because of currency restrictions, through no fault of the Canadian government. I could not be too critical of the present administration if they were not able to get back there. But I would be very critical of them, and I am sure everybody on the Atlantic coast would be very critical if they were not trying very hard, using every possible device they can think of in negotiations to that end.
The minister said a few words about the European market, and he was kind enough to make a rather flattering reference to a speech I made, as well as to the excellent speech

Supply-Trade and Commerce made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo who knows far more about the fishing industry than I do.
There is one brief suggestion I made yesterday that I should like to repeat to the minister today. I imagine this suggestion would actually require to be implemented through the Department of Fisheries. The minister talked about the shortage of fish for the European market. It is quite true that the quality of fish required for the Spanish and the Italian markets, which pay a better price than does any other market for salt fish, has been short the last two or three years, since Mr. Winters made his visit to Europe and negotiated the increased market there. I urged upon my colleagues in the previous administration,-without success, I admit-I urge upon the minister, and I intend to urge upon the Minister of Fisheries, that we should adopt a system of premiums for this high quality fish for a few years in the hope of having the production kept up and possibly expanded until such time as the technical and economic problem of making that improved fish in fish plants is completely solved.
The minister will perhaps recall that before the war, when we were seeking to get into the market in the United Kingdom-I know my leader knows a great deal about this matter-for bacon and cheese premiums were used very successfully to expand the Canadian production rapidly in order to get that larger fraction of United Kingdom markets which we had in those days and about which the minister spoke earlier. It seems to me that that device, which we know through experience worked very well in the case of bacon and cheese, would probably work well also in the case of this high quality fish.

A moment ago the minister made a comment I believe in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The reference was first to aluminum and whether there were any other commodities with regard to which Russia had been able to underprice us and undersell us and thus affect what may have been traditional Canadian markets. He mentioned lumber particularly as having suffered because of lower prices being offered by the Soviet union in what were traditionally our markets. I wonder first whether the minister could expand that statement that our lumber exports have suffered by mentioning the markets which we have lost or in which our sales have dropped as a result of Russian sales of lumber.
I have not that information readily available. I would have to have it looked up and perhaps give a report to the hon. member at a later time.

I should like to make one other comment in that regard. It arises not only out of the answer just given by the minister to this specific question but out of other answers of a similar type. Would the minister not consider that it would probably be more advisable to follow the lead of his colleagues and arrange to have departmental officials here to advise him on some of these detailed questions which may arise.
Yes; but I am waiting until we get past this first item and I am hoping now that the hon. member is suggesting that we move on,-
It is not a suggestion to move on, it is a suggestion to get some information.

-that we may move on past the first item. The procedure is to have officials here in order to provide answers to the specific questions which are asked, not on the first item on which there is general discussion but when hon. members start asking specific questions on lumber or something like that. I think the hon. member is suggesting the officials should be here.
I should like to point out that the minister himself raised the question of lumber in the first place.
But I did not ask a question about it.

This is I think a general question. In rising I should like to bring the minister back to the West Indies and to his trip there in May when he was attending the ceremony on the birthday of the West Indies federation and when at a press conference he is reported as being asked by a correspondent of the London Times whether Canada regarded the West Indies as their protege rather than Britain's.	The report
goes on to say that the Hon. Gordon Churchill gave an answer that added up to the view that Canada did regard the West Indies as its protege rather than Britain's. Would the minister like to comment on that very important statement?

It is a very important statement, Mr. Chairman; and my friend the Leader of the Opposition, with his fine experience of press conferences, knows perfectly well that this is a fabricated answer because it says that my answer added up to such and such. It did not say that I said it directly, and of course I did not say it at all.

There are one or two general matters with which I want to deal before we move on from item No. 1. They arise out of the minister's remarks this afternoon. The first one has to do with the discussion about the proposal of the chancellor of the exchequer of the United Kingdom for free trade between Canada and the United Kingdom. In dealing with all that had been said about that matter yesterday and this morning by hon. members on the opposition side of the house, the minister disposed of it rather quickly; and as I understood his remarks and tried to note them down, he tried to liken that proposal to a suggestion put forward in the same way by the Leader of the Opposition about the Atlantic area trade, and he left the whole matter there. I think it should be pointed out to hon. members that the proposal for free trade between the United Kingdom and Canada was put forward by the chancellor of the exchequer of the United Kingdom at a conference called by the Canadian government to decide whether or not a commonwealth trade conference should be held.
