At that conference I think all the commonwealth countries were represented by their ministers, or nearly all of them; and it is quite a different matter than a suggestion made in a speech in the house here. It is something that I do not think he should brush aside quite so lightly as he has done.
The second point I want to deal with is this. Yesterday and again today the minister dealt with the balance of trade between certain areas; that is between Canada and the United States and between Canada and the sterling bloc or the United Kingdom. In both his speech yesterday and again today he made a rather flattering reference-and I think properly so-to a speech made by the hon. member who spoke last night on balance of payments.

The hon. member for
Rosthern.
No.
The hon. member for Macleod.

Yes, the hon. member for Macleod. I want to draw to the attention of the minister one omission in his speech yesterday in relation to this subject and to find out whether there is any significance in it. I noted it yesterday when he was delivering it but I did not refer to it earlier. As reported at page 2321 of Hansard, the second column, the minister, in talking about the pattern of trade, goes on to give, for example, the commodity exports to Great Britain, the commodity exports to other commonwealth
Supply-Trade and Commerce countries and to the United States. Then in the next paragraph he refers to imports from Great Britain rising by two per cent and imports from the United States falling. Then in the next paragraph he went on to say this:
The trade figures that I have given are indicative of three developments. First, Canada's foreign trade with the world as a whole has been maintained-
And so on. Then he says this:
Second, a certain measure of diversification and expansion of trade has taken place leading to a better balance in our trade pattern.
What concerns me is that the minister in dealing with the item gave the exports to three areas, namely the United Kingdom, the remainder of the commonwealth and the United States. He then gave the imports from two of those areas, the United States and the United Kingdom. Imports from the U.S. have of course dropped and that would make an apparent improvement in the balance of commodity trade with that area. Exports to the U.K. have risen, which would also make an apparent improvement in the blance with that country. But the minister omitted to deal with the second part of the problem. He failed completely to refer to imports from the remainder of the commonwealth, and I would respectfully suggest to the minister that if he is going to make a distinction between the rest of the commonwealth and the United Kingdom he should have elaborated a little further. If the minister will refer to the weekly bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics dated Friday, July 11, 1958 he will find in the second last paragraph on page 9 these words:
Imports from the United Kingdom reached $116,200,000 in the first quarter of 1958, some 2 per cent higher than in the first quarter of 1957.
Then the first sentence of the last paragraph reads:
Canadian imports from the commonwealth fell about $36 million in the first three months of 1958, some 14 per cent below their 1957 level.
What I would like to know from the minister is the reason why he dealt with the three areas in respect of export figures and only two of them in respect of import figures. Is it because he is seeking to balance the trade with each country individually or what was the reason for the rather noticeable omission?
The third matter which I wish to deal with arises out of the discussion this afternoon about the 15 per cent diversion of imports from the U.S. to the U.K., which was brushed aside rather hastily by the minister. I think it is well to place on record some of the newspaper references to this matter which are rather interesting. It will be seen that these Canadian newspapers are important ones. I

Supply-Trade and Commerce think one or two of the many such references will serve to illustrate why I believe the Canadian, British and other people are entitled to believe that the Prime Minister and the government meant what they apparently said on the occasions when they advocated a policy of diverting 15 per cent of our imports from the U.S. to the U.K. Firstly, the London Times of July 8, 1957, carried an article, part of which I will quote as follows:
Mr. Diefenbaker, the Canadian Prime Minister, told a press conference yesterday on his return from the commonwealth conference in London that Canada has as a planned objective the diversion of 15 per cent of her present imports from the United States to imports from the United Kingdom.
Then the Ottawa Journal of the same date had this to say:
The diversion of 15 per cent of Canadian buying to the British market would make "a substantial improvement" in trade with the United Kingdom without damaging business relations with the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I have mentioned this on more than one occasion, but I do not mind the repetition over and over again of a song that was sung throughout the election campaign. Hear, hear.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, July 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Taylor for the second reading of Bill No. S-4, respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Regier.

maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that I had just taken the floor in the debate on this bill on Friday, July 4, before six o'clock. I hope that I will be able to clear up in a few moments some of the misconceptions that were apparently held by some hon. members at that time.
57071-3-152
Private Bills
To refresh our memories I might state briefly that the bill deals with a toll bridge which runs between the cities of Vancouver and North Vancouver and the purpose of the bill is to make provision for the payment of remuneration to the directors of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company and reimbursing them for their expenses in the performance of their services as directors. The shares of the company are held by the municipalities concerned and the city of Vancouver. Since that time I have taken a look at other bridge companies. There are about 250 tunnel and bridge companies in Canada incorporated under dominion charter since confederation and I cannot find one other instance in all of those bridge companies where no provision is made for the directors to be paid. That in itself is a pretty good indication that this is a reasonable and straightforward request.
The second point I wish to deal with is that some of the members brought up the interest of the taxpayers, in as much as this bridge and its shares are held by the municipalities concerned. I think that is one of the very good reasons why we should pass this bill, because we are not deciding here that these directors are going to be paid. The municipalities as shareholders will actually have the right to authorize payment. We are not saying that they are going to receive so much pay. They are setting a very low limit as to what they can be paid and that is contained in the bill. The maximum is $500 a year for a director and a slightly higher amount for the chairman of the board. Also, some other hon. members felt that this board should be compared with some of the other boards of city councils. For instance, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) had this to say as reported at page 1946 of Hansard:
Being elected members they are in the same position as others with similar responsibilities.
He was referring to the fact that all of the members of the board of directors are also members of the city and municipal councils which are involved. He continued:
If you are a member of a city council, a municipal council or a rural municipal council your work is designated by the council. You may be called upon to serve on a library board, a sewer board and undertake all the various responsibilities that go with election to office. Quite bluntly, I cannot see why there should be any differentiation between the responsibilities of a member of a council serving on a library board or sewer board and those of a director of a bridge company engaged in rendering a service.
Since that time I have received from one of the aldermen of the city of Vancouver certain information in this respect in which he states that he has sat on the greater

Private Bills
Vancouver water board and also on the greater Vancouver sewerage board and for that service he has received $15 a meeting, and those meetings often take place more than once a month, which would mean perhaps that he would be receiving $30 a month or some $360 a year in remuneration on that basis. He also states that he has put in considerably more time on the bridge board than he has ever put in on the other boards involved. Therefore, it becomes apparent that even if the maximum rate were put into effect the men would not be overpaid.
I hope that this will clear up some of the misconceptions, because members of those other boards are paid and also, as I have pointed out, all of the other bridge authorities from one end of Canada to the other pay their directors. I did not look over the entire 250 but I did look through 50 or 60 of them and in many instances it was stated in the charter that provision was made for the municipalities to take them over. There was the understanding that some of them might be municipally owned but still there was provision for the directors to be paid. In the light of the new facts that we have to go on, it will be seen that there is no need for the amendment that is before us and this bill could be properly passed.

maintopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up the time of the house for more than two or three minutes. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) moved his amendment in good faith in order to protect the taxpayers of the municipalities. Since this bill was first discussed-I do wish that when it was brought up more information had been available to hon. members-I have received more information and other Vancouver members have also received information which should make it quite clear that this is not asking for anything to which we should not agree.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) has said, other municipal boards, the Vancouver sewerage board and the water board, pay the members of the board on an honorarium basis. School boards on which I have served are quite free to pay themselves if they so wish. The criterion in this bill is that the municipalities themselves own all the shares in the bridge and they would have to authorize payment. All that we are being asked to do is to make it possible for the municipalities if they so wish to do so. They are free to pay the directors within the limit stipulated within the bill. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment should be withdrawn but if the hon. member is not willing to withdraw it we should defeat it, pass the bill and leave to the

municipalities concerned the right to run their own affairs instead of our trying to tell them what they can or cannot do.

Mr. Speaker, I have just one comment or two. The last two hon. members who have participated in this debate, especially the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), indicated that some additional information had been received which would warrant the withdrawal of the amendment to refer it to a committee first. But with no indication as to what this additional information is, where it emanated from, what effect it would have on clearing up our lack of understanding and that expressed by members of the Conservative party when the bill was being debated on another day; with no clear indication from the councils of the municipalities owning practically all the shares in the bridge and tunnel company, we cannot properly be expected to agree to withdraw the motion for referral to a committee first. He said: Mr. Speaker, if I may, I should like to outline just briefly the purpose of this bill. The Canadian Pacific railway over a period of years have assumed control over a number of subsidiaries which have been embodied in the C.P.R. system. In order to simplify the corporate organization of the C.P.R., they wish to dissolve these companies as subsidiaries and to take over the assets and the liabilities of the companies as outlined in the bill. This is the third project. They have already done this with respect to two other groups, in 1956 when 13 were dissolved and in 1957 when 14 were dissolved. I may make it quite clear that they are still maintaining the same services, they are employing their own men on these railways and there will be no change in the employment of the people concerned. It is a matter of reorganization for administrative purposes. I also want to state to the house that when this bill is referred to the committee the officials of the company will be present to answer any questions that any hon. members might have in respect of these companies. Of the nine companies mentioned here, seven are dominion companies and will be dissolved by this act. The other companies are provincial companies and would have to be dealt with by the provincial jurisdiction. This act deals with the assets and liabilities of these companies in so far as the dominion jurisdiction extends to them.

Mr. Speaker, while we in this group fully appreciate the explanation given by the hon. member with respect to the purpose of this bill which, according to the explanatory note, is to simplify the corporate organization of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, on behalf of this group I want to say a word or two.
These bills coming before the house to cancel the charters of various subsidiaries and to bring them within the terms of the

Private Bills
parent company indicate the number of charters that were granted years ago to these railway companies throughout Canada. Only two sessions ago, I think it was, we had a number of bills with the same purpose with respect to a number of railways in British Columbia. I occasionally look up the grants these various railway companies have received in the way of land, money and things of that sort. Anyone who reads the history of railway development in Canada realizes that the Canadian Pacific railway and all the subsidiaries that are now being incorporated or brought within the fold of the company did very well in the early days with respect to grants of land or cash from the federal government or, in some cases, from the provincial government.
I think these bills to simplify the corporate organization of the C.P.R. clearly indicate a certain trend in this country. We are not going to oppose this bill because we realize that under these circumstances this is the common sense thing to do. However, we are taking this opportunity to bring a few things to the attention of the house. I think it was two sessions ago that we had another bill that provided for the abandonment of a certain portion of the C.P.R. between Kaslo and New Denver and at that time as a sort of carrot held out to local people was the fact that the government of British Columbia was going to take over the right of way and use it as a standard highway and so on. To date there has been no action in that respect. Consequently that portion of the district has been completely without rail services or highway services satisfactory for the hauling out of mining commodities since that time.
Not only these bills to simplify the corporate organization of the C.P.R. but those to abandon certain sections of the railway in certain parts of Canada and also to reduce services as has been done on the Kettle Valley railway in recent months-a situation which we tried to correct by introducing in this house a bill which was unfortunately defeated-we presume are efforts to lower costs because of changing circumstances in Canada. As far as we are concerned, they all indicate a fluid and uncertain situation in Canada with respect to railway transportation.
From the point of view of this group, we think that all these measures to simplify the corporate organization of the C.P.R., to abandon certain sections of the line entirely and to reduce service on other sections of the line indicate the necessity for a national transportation policy which we in this group have urged for many years. We consider that railways are a very important utility-possibly the most important one-linking all regions in Canada, and certainly very necessary for
[Mr. Herridge.l
the transportation of goods produced in this country from one point to another. It is for that reason that the C.C.F. believe in the necessity for an over-all national transportation policy as a result of action by the government of Canada which will integrate our rail, water, air and road transportation to the end that we may have some logical development of our transportation services so that we are able to provide the people of Canada with adequate and necessary transportation services at the lowest cost possible having regard to the national needs of Canada, and the people of Canada first. Second, we in the C.C.F. believe that a national transportation policy would be to the advantage of the employees of the railway companies of this country and to the employees of the other transportation agencies.
In that connection, before resuming my seat, I also wish to illustrate the need for some sort of over-all transportation policy and control so far as developments, extensions, roads and pensions are concerned. We all know that the pensioners of the C.P.R. who retired prior to January 1, 1953, have been asking for amendment of their pensions. These long service railroaders are being denied justice at the present time because they are pensioned at a very much lower rate than are those who were pensioned after January 1, 1953. speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, July 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Broome for the second reading of Bill No. S-6, respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it appears that the fates are not operating very kindly for me, for upon reflection it seems to me that last week when I made a few comments on this matter it was at about this time and I did not get the opportunity to conclude my remarks. I hope I will be able to do so today.
Last week at about six o'clock the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), the sponsor of this bill, directed a question to me which I was unable to grasp at the time. Upon looking at Hansard for July 11 and reading the question, I hope I am now in a position to answer. The question asked as recorded at page 2183 of Hansard for that date was as follows:
Will the hon. member permit a question? Is he not aware that not one cent was made in promotion fees in the promotion of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company?
Then, I expect in explanation he continued:
In reading the prospectus I tried to point out that every cent raised went into the treasury of the company and was used for the development of the company.
I suppose the hon. member's question arose out of my remarks just preceding his question, which were with reference to the fact that the oil and gas pipe line industry in general was a most lucrative one, with which I am sure he will not disagree. At that time I had no specific reference to the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. It was a general reference to the industry and the profitable state in which that industry had been for many years, both here in Canada and particularly in the United States.
Following those remarks as to the lucrative state of the industry both with respect to oil and gas pipe lines and the public services which such pipe lines provide, I was leading up to the opinions expressed by other members of the C.C.F., both verbally and in formal form by motion in the year

1951 when the company was originally incorporated. For the benefit of hon. members who have not read the history of this company, we offered the suggestion that this particular pipe line company, inasmuch as it did provide a public service, should be operated under public ownership, the same solution as we suggested should be applied to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines in the years later than 1951. At that time, in 1951, with respect to this company, and in later years with respect to the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company, we in the C.C.F. could foresee the present state of events, and while there have been tremendous earnings and tremendous profits in this particular company there has probably not been the type of stock market manipulation which has taken place with respect to the gas pipe lines industry where, probably, the reasons for public ownership are even more pronounced than they are here. That was the trend of my remarks which occasioned the hon. member for Vancouver South to ask his question, and X am sure that if he will read in Hansard what I said he will realize that there was no need to have directed that question to me, and that the matter does not require any more extended answer than I gave in my explanatory remarks.
An idea of the resources and the profit making capacity of this company has already been placed on the record, together with the number of shares placed on the market. At one time I understand they cost in the neighbourhood of $140 a share compared with $10 when they were originally put on the market and at the time these shares were being sold on the market for $140 this company approached parliament with the selfsame bill asking for the same thing that they are asking now, that is, in effect a stock split of five to one by an increase in the number of shares which they might issue. Apparently the reasons advanced last year in favour of this proposal do not differ too greatly from those which the officials of the company are putting forward at this time, namely that the price of the shares on the market when they were at $140 a share was too high and that if additional shares were put on the market for sale the company would have a difficult time selling them to the general public because few people would care to pay $140 for a share in Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company when there was every possibility that the price of the shares might decline and that they could be bought later on at a lower price. By splitting five to one, or by increasing the number of shares that the company may issue, the $140 divided by five would equal $28-this was one year ago-and the shares then, if this bill had

been proceeded with a year ago, would have been reduced to $28 a share on the market.
We find, now, that if that same reasoning of the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company were to be applied to the request for a change in their capital structure this year, they should properly not have asked for a five to one split but only for a two to one split. I do not know what the actual price of these shares is today, but it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50 to $60. If the reasoning was that the company wanted these shares to get down to, say, $28 when they were selling at $140, then, surely, when they are selling at between $50 and $60, to get them down on the market to a share price in the area of $28 we can reasonably assume that they should have asked for a two to one stock split.
I wonder why the company still requires a five to one division now. If their reasoning was valid a year ago they should either have asked for a greater increase in the stock split ratio before or for a lesser increase now in order to keep their thoughts now in tune with what they were a year ago. Now when the officials of this company undertook to meet with those of us in the C.C.F. party who had expressed some interest in this particular bill, they answered a number of questions and made a number of general comments, and if my memory serves me right the figure I jotted down indicated that they had put on the market on their original capitalization-and if I am incorrect I am sure I will be corrected-1,500,000 shares, or something in that neighbourhood, as of 1956, and as of today that same amount is out and the company has not issued any more shares from its treasury.
We asked the officials at that time whether, if they had put more shares on the market out of the original five million shares which the company issued that would not have had some effect on holding down the number of the shares.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before this item carries may I say that when we left it at five o'clock we had been subjected by the Prime Minister to some interesting observations concerning the 15 per cent diversion proposal, a matter about which he seems to be exceedingly sensitive. All I want to say about that is, as was said by the hon. member for Ottawa West, that everybody in Canada who read about it in the newspapers, everybody in the United States or in the United Kingdom who read about it in the newspapers, thought there was such a proposal and referred to it as such. It was allowed to be considered as a proposal during the election campaign and it accomplished its purpose presumably at that time and now it is to be forgotten and we are not supposed to mention it. Apparently the election decided that diversion should die. The first obituary notice that I discovered was in a United States magazine, the U. S. News and World Report. As a matter of fact, I think I have come across not only the obituary notice of this proposal but its birth notice. It lived from 1953 until 1958, because on July 10, 1953, speaking in Red Deer Hill, Alberta, the Prime Minister is reported by the Prince Albert Herald as having said, and I quote from this newspaper account of the statement he made at that time:
Britain could buy Canadian products if she had the dollars-15 per cent of Canada's present defence needs are being purchased in the United States, but should be bought in the United Kingdom, as well as heavy machinery.
This was in 1953. There is the birth of the 15 per cent proposal, which has now apparently died.
There is one other matter, though, Mr. Chairman, that I want to bring up before we leave this item because I am not clear in my own mind as to what is the situation actually, although the minister did his best this afternoon to explain it. It is in connection with the list of prohibited exports to China. The minister said this afternoon that that list had been made public in January, 1957, and that if any member of the committee wants to find out what goods are on that prohibited list and, therefore, not eligible for export to communist China under present conditions all he has to do is read the list. But it was my impression

and the minister will correct me if I am wrong about this and I think it is a matter of some importance- that at that time there was a list of prohibited goods for China which was more extensive than the list of prohibited goods for Russia and that international discussions began to remove that differential in 1957.
What I should like to ask the minister is, are these discussions still going on? Are we obliged to take no action in regard to the

Supply-Trade and Commerce reduction of that list of prohibited goods until we get agreement with all the members of the commission in Paris. Are any other members of that group-most of them are NATO countries-and particularly is the United Kingdom, observing the same list of prohibited exports to China as we are, or is our list the same as that of the United States but not the same as that of some other countries? What is the exact position in regard to that matter? If the minister is not in a position to give me details of that matter at the present moment perhaps he might be able to do it later when he has his officials before him.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Just a comment, Mr. Chairman; my understanding is that the prohibited China list was much more extensive at one time than the list in so far as other communist countries were concerned, but that within recent months, or within the last year, there was no dissimilarity between the two lists. Then, we moved a step farther and conferences that are now taking place are aimed at reducing the items on the list still farther.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
In view of the rather
lengthy discussion about trade with China yesterday and today, I wonder whether the minister would care to give the committee any information that he feels he can about the Chinese group who are in Canada at the present time apparently on a buying or selling mission. In this morning's Montreal Gazette I found a story headed up: "Red China winds up city tour." The article refers to their presence in Montreal. There have been other similar types of stories in the papers in the last few days.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I have been informed that two representatives from China have been in Canada for some time and are here for the purposes of trade, representing some, if not all, of the state trading corporations in China, of which there are 16, and that these gentlemen have visited various cities in Canada. I think they were in Ottawa about two weeks ago and are in Montreal at the present time and are engaged in a buying and selling mission. I have heard that they were interested in the subject of wheat and my hope is that perhaps they will find it possible to make arrangements for the purchase of another cargo of Canadian wheat. That is all I know with regard to them. I think there are two of them. Are there more than two mentioned in the article?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: No, just the two.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: That is all I know about these two gentlemen who are in Canada at the present time.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Again on China, the minister said last evening that the jurisdiction of the trade commissioner in Hong Kong-if "jurisdiction" is the right word-extends to continental China-that is communist China- as well as to certain other territories, including Taiwan. I should like to ask the minister whether it is contemplated that the trade commissioner in Hong Kong will make, as part of his routine duties, periodic trips to continental China as is normally the case with trade commissioners in respect of territories which they cover and whether the Chinese government in Peking accepts our trade commissioner's trade credentials, not diplomatic but trade credentials, over the territory in question of the communist government of China.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I think that as a result of his visit there last fall and arising from the contacts he made with the heads and representatives of the trading corporations in the four cities he visited Mr. Forsyth-Smith will go back to China, continue his investigations and continue to maintain close relations with those who are so actively engaged in trade. I do not know what his plans are at the moment but it would appear to me to be quite worth while that he should do so. In his messages back home he has repeatedly urged that Canadian businessmen visit Hong Kong and China and get acquainted with the representatives of these trading corporations. They have offices in Hong Kong in addition to their headquarters in Peking, Canton, Shanghai and so on. He feels that by making personal contacts our Canadian businessmen might be able to enlarge our business in China and that this would be best done in that manner. I suppose the point of contact for our Canadian businessmen would first be in Hong Kong with Mr. Forsyth-Smith who could then advise them as to what course of action to follow after that.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I first of all thank the minister for answering, in the course of his remarks this afternoon, a question which has been bothering me for quite some time relative to the importation into Canada of tractors from the United States which are originally made in Great Britain. Has the minister given any consideration to the suggestion I made that the government, through the high commissioner in London, might conceivably encourage the Massey-Harris-Ferguson Company in Great Britain to have the tractors that are used in the Canadian market assembled in Canada rather than Canada purchasing such tractors from the United States?

The amount of money spent on the tractors imported from the United States is considerable, something like $150 million, and the financial situation would not be changed in any way. Great Britain would get the same amount of return and I believe it would create employment in Canada if these tractors were assembled in this country rather than in the United States. I wonder whether the minister might, through the high commissioner in London encourage Massey-Harris-Ferguson to make use of its subsidiaries in Canada for the assembling of these tractors in this country.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I should like to thank the hon. gentleman for what appears to be a very useful suggestion and I will see that the matter is taken up with the appropriate officials in London.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if he recalls the approximate date-I do not mean the exact date-he first saw one of the documents prepared in his department for official use and for the use of the minister entitled, "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1957?"

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I find it very difficult to recall the date. I was rather busily engaged last fall in certain travels but I think it was perhaps late in the fall that it came to my attention. I could not take my oath on the date at all. Whether it was November, December or January I am not in a position to state.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Then the minister did not see this document before preparations were made for the Mont Tremblant conference? One would have thought that this would be the kind of document that the minister would use in preparation for that conference and I wondered whether that might perhaps assist him in recalling.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
The difficulty there is that the Mont Tremblant conference took place just at the end of September. In the early part of September I was out west for two or three days making a speech at the annual meeting of the dairy council. That was followed by two or three days inspecting the northern Ontario gas pipe line. On my return to Ottawa I left after a very short interval for a ten-day trip to England and Europe. I recall getting back here on a Friday at noon and leaving by plane for Mont Tremblant at 2.30 with a brief case filled with documents. That document may have been in the brief case but I had very little opportunity to make the type of preparation for the Mont Tremblant conference that it
Supply-Trade and Commerce required. Under those circumstances my memory fails me whether or not the document was there or whether I had time to read it if it was there.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Supply-Trade and Commerce carried on in the cabinet-I am not attempting to penetrate the secrets of the cabinet at all-it would have been very logical, and perhaps very obvious, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to have received that documentation in his department. A decision of this importance, particularly a decision made by a government which had campaigned throughout the country on the basis of doubling the modest immigration program we had up to that time, I can only assume was a very serious and grave decision, and that all the possible information that might be brought to bear upon it was brought to bear upon it.
I do feel, therefore, it would be of some interest to know at what date the minister considered that document, and at what date he had begun the planning of the administration of his department in relation to the information contained in that document which we were told, on an occasion last January, was a document of transcendent importance and which revealed all that was going to happen in the economy of Canada for the rest of the year. It does, I think, cast a rather curious reflection upon the minister's administration of his department in the first five or six months he was minister that he is unable to recollect when he first saw this document which contained this startling information that the Prime Minister revealed to us in such dramatic fashion in January.
Another reason, of course, for my curiosity about this matter is that we were assured- perhaps it would hardly be in order for me to go this far afield-by the Prime Minister at the time of the federal-provincial conference in November, and we were assured by the Minister of Labour as late as December 10, 1957 in most categorical fashion, that all was rosy with the Canadian economy. There does seem to be a good deal of evidence, to which the minister has contributed a little more this evening, that the government, apart from the Minister of Justice who admitted quite frankly he had the information, seems to have been extraordinarily unaware of the situation which burst upon them with such dramatic suddenness in January. I do not know whether, in the light of what I have recalled to the minister's mind, I have assisted him at all in his recollections.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Following up this matter a little bit, Mr. Chairman, the minister will remember, as we remember, how bitterly we on this side were attacked last January by the Prime Minister because we kept secret the contents of this report in 1957, to which my hon. friend has referred. We hid it, and that was a dastardly crime to parliament and to the public. It became the hidden report. We refused to make it public
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
at that time, and that was our sin and our crime.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The Minister of Justice compounded the felony.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I am very anxious to free the minister from the possibility of any such accusation in respect of the report for 1958, the report which has now been completed and is in the possession of the government, and on the conclusions of which no doubt the Minister of Finance based, in part at least, his economic and financial calculations for his budget. So that the minister may not be subject to this accusation of hiding a report from parliament, I wonder whether he would take advantage of this opportunity to give us some information about the conclusions of the report which is now in the possession of the government and which deals with the present fiscal year?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I am very grateful, Mr. Chairman, for the solicitude shown by the Leader of the Opposition for my integrity, and the care he takes about my future in regard to this report. My recollection is, however, that the Prime Minister, in response to a question asked in the house several weeks ago, gave the appropriate answer concerning this report and other reports of a confidential nature which circulate within the departments of government.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Yes, the Prime Minister said it would not be proper to table this report or make it public until January, 1959. But, the Prime Minister attacked us very bitterly and vehemently because we did not make public the report for 1957 in the spring and summer of 1957. If we were wrong in concealing that report at that time, is the government not wrong in concealing at this time this report for the next year?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I thought that the accusation levelled at the former administration was that, having the knowledge contained in that celebrated report, they failed to act upon it and misled the people.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Oh, no, Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend will read the record of that debate he will find that the charge was that we kept that report hidden. We heard about it not only in the House of Commons but all over the country during the election campaign. It was a crime against the public interest to have kept that report hidden; that is how it got the name "hidden report". So what about the report for this year?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: You told the Canadian people the opposite.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: What about the report for this year? Is it in a different category?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Are you not misleading the people of Canada now?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The economic survey for 1958 will be studied very carefully, and has been studied very carefully, and the government, in its judgment, will act in accordance with that report, as we thought the former government should have done.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
On that point, I convict the minister out of the mouth of the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice admitted quite unequivocally in the passage I read from Hansard, that one of the senior members of the government-I do not believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce would deny his influence as a member of the government-not only had but acted upon that information in July. In other words, if there was anything wrong about our attitude to that report before June, surely it was much more wrong for the government and for the Minister of Justice to have kept it hidden after it was discovered in late June, and for the Minister of Justice to have failed to tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce what was in it or to tell the Minister of Labour what was in it, instead of letting him go on giving these rosy pictures of the economy which were given by the Prime Minister to the premiers of the provinces when they were here in November, and which were given in public utterances by the Minister of Labour, the member of the government having the special responsibility for unemployment.
So if there is any kind of charge that when we received this report in March we did not act upon it, a charge which is totally false, incidentally-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Well, anyone who will make an honest and careful comparison of that document with Mr. Harris' budget speech will see that Mr. Harris very faithfully reproduced in his budget speech the conclusions of that document. What the Prime Minister did do, in the most shocking piece of misrepresentation this parliament has ever seen, was to take bits and pieces out of that document to deceive the public for political purposes.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
There are two matters that I should like the hon. member to confirm, he having been so close to the administration at the time. Did that report state or did it not that heavy unemployment was anticipated? The second question is this. Did not
Supply-Trade and Commerce the election pamphlets of 1957 say "Vote St. Laurent for More Jobs"?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I could look the matter up very quickly for the hon. member. It forecast exactly what happened. It stated that it was expected that employment would increase all through 1957 and employment did increase all through 1957.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Because there was a change in government.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen who are making these unintelligent noises will look at the statistics they will find that all during 1957 employment did increase.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY

We are not really discussing the resolution when we are discussing the record of the Liberal administration of years past.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Not at all, Mr. Chairman. What I was discussing was a document issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and introduced into this parliament by the Prime Minister. I was attempting to find out when the minister, the present incumbent of that office, took cognizance of that document which the Prime Minister himself said was the most important economic document prepared for the previous government and available to them when they came into office. Surely nothing could be more relevant to the discussion of the estimates and the administration of the department by the minister than the question as to whether the minister, after he took office, spent his time travelling around the country, getting off one plane and getting into another, or whether he spent some time familiarizing himself with the duties of his office.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If I may continue my reply to the hon. member for York-Scarborough, I was saying that this was a forecast. That is all this document was, a sort of economic weather forecast. The gentleman who prepared this document was well trained. I have no doubt about that. speechtext: What about Harris?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If I may continue, Mr. Chairman, to answer the hon. member for York-Scarborough, may I say that what that document forecast was that employment would continue to rise throughout 1957 but that the rate of increase might be slower than it had been in 1956. That is precisely what happened.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: That is not how you described it last January.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I did not catch that remark.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: That is not how you described it last January.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: How I described what last January?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The unemployment situation.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The unemployment situation last January was, as the Prime Minister himself admitted, becoming very serious.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The hon. member for York-Scarborough apparently was not listening as attentively as he usually does because I was talking about employment. I was not talking about unemployment. There is no doubt that unemployment did increase much more rapidly than there was any ground for expecting it to increase on the basis of that so-called hidden report. There are some of us who feel that part of the reason why it increased more rapidly than was expected was because of a certain event that happened last June.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Leaving that report and returning to the current report which is certainly in order because it deals with the work of the department this year, I wonder whether the minister would give us some indication of the conclusions of this economic report from his department and more particularly tell us whether it agrees with the Minister of Finance's budgetary statement that
[The Chairman.]
our gross national product will increase by 2 per cent while our price level will remain constant during the year, and, in general, the economic trends that it forecasts. I am sure that information would be very interesting to the house and perhaps very important.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If the Leader of the Opposition has reached the conclusion that the Minister of Finance based some of his budget remarks on the report to which reference has been made, I think the question now put should be put before the Minister of Finance. I do not think I am called upon to explain the connection, if any, between one report and another. I would hope that the ancient report of 1957, allegedly twice lost or hidden, might now be buried, that the 1958 report might be safely left where it is, and that perhaps we could get on with questions dealing with trade and commerce.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to get back to the Soviet trade offensive for a moment or two, if I can, and get away from the hidden sins of both the Liberal party and the Conservative party. I do not see any difference between hiding a report in 1957 and hiding it in 1958. Sometime ago we learned of a letter that was sent by the Soviet premier, Nikita Khrushchev, to the President of the United States proposing a tremendous increase in trade between the United States and Russia. According to Premier Krushchev's letter he envisaged trade of several billion dollars. I should like to know whether there has been any consultation or exchange of notes between the government of Canada and the Soviet union as to increasing trade between our two countries. What study is the government making on improving or increasing the amount of trade between Canada and Russia? Has a similar proposal been made to Canada? I think we will all agree-and certainly the Americans agreed, although they turned it down

that it was a very important and far-reaching proposal and that it was another indication of the all-out Soviet trade offensive. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that we in this group believe that the government should do everything possible to increase trade with all nations of the world in non-strategic goods. I would hope that the minister would be able to give the committee a fairly comprehensive report on just what Canada is doing to increase trade with this very large and important nation?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
There has been no exchange of notes of a nature similar to the one to which my hon. friend refers, so far as I know, between Canada and Russia. We are actively interested in expanding our trade everywhere in the world, as I have stated on so many

occasions. We have had conversations with the Russian representatives here in Ottawa with regard to expanding trade between our two countries. We have had from time to time reports from businessmen who have visited Russia with regard to the possibility of enlarging Canada's trade with that country.
I think we have been quite active so far as Russia is concerned and we are quite prepared to trade with that country. We have in fact had a fairly satisfactory deal with Russia in respect to wheat during the last two or three years.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could say whether any substantial official trade delegation to the Soviet union has been considered. There was some discussion some time ago as to whether the minister himself might make a trip to China this fall, and I believe the Prime Minister was rather non-commital in this respect. I wonder if the government has given this matter any consideration, and I would hope it has, with respect to the sending of a trade delegation to Asia, particularly to China and the Soviet union. I would think if Canada received an offer in somewhat similar terms to that made by Premier Khrushchev to the United States it would be advisable for Canada to consider such an offer as a serious one and to negotiate with the Soviet union on the basis of such an offer because at the present time with the widespread unemployment in this country, any very large increase in Canada's exports would help to restore full employment. I hope the government, and the minister in particular, are giving consideration to this idea.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
The second part of my hon. friend's question was hypothetical. It had something to do with "if a similar note came, would we do something about it".
The first part of his question was whether or not I was contemplating a visit or was arranging for an official trade mission to Russia and the answer to that is no, not at the present time. We have in mind and are considering various visits but have not yet reached a decision as to where such visits should be made. The important thing to consider in undertaking trade missions or visits on the part of the officials and the minister of this department is as to where we can get the greatest advantage, tradewise from those visits. Now it sounds interesting to talk about China or Russia but there are other parts of the world where our trading relations have been closer and where our trade is greater and where trade expansion might be more easily achieved. All these factors will be taken into account before any decision is reached as to where missions from Canada may be sent.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I would hope, Mr. Chairman, in the light of the world situation at this time and in view of the great need for expanded markets the minister himself would very seriously consider heading up an official Canadian delegation to China and the Soviet union in order to discuss the possibilities of a vast expansion of trade between Canada and those countries. I would now like to ask the minister to comment on a report in tonight's Citizen by Bruce Phillips which in part states as follows:
U.S. officials in Ottawa will ask their government to lift import quotas against Canadian oil.
Diplomatic sources say U.S. embassy staff here have undergone a change of outlook on the subject of import controls, and will make their views known in Washington.
They have, apparently, accepted the Canadian government's contention that Canada's oil represents a vital source of supply in terms of continental defence, and should therefore be exempt from import barriers.
Could the minister say whether the government is making progress in this regard and does he hold forth hopes of the so-called voluntary restrictions possibly being lifted soon?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It is obvious from the article that the government has been making great progress and I do hold out great hopes.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: In the course of his remarks this afternoon the minister said that our lumber exports have suffered from Soviet competition. I would like the minister to answer this question, and I am sure he can do so without the assistance of his officials because it has nothing to do with statistics. The economy of the Atlantic provinces is closely related to the export of pulpwood and pit props. We all realize that in recent months, especially in the last 12 months, the export of pit props to the European market has dropped considerably and we are told that even Great Britain, with whom we are anxious to increase our trade, is buying its pulpwood and pit props from Russia and from countries under Russian domination.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: And from Finland.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Could the minister tell us what action is being taken by the government with respect to instructing his department to try to bring back to normal the export of pulpwood and pit props from the maritime provinces.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I took a very active interest in the question of pit props which were exported in considerable quantity from the maritime provinces and last fall, when the president of the board of trade from the United Kingdom was in this country with his officials, we discussed this matter. Subsequently when I was in England

Supply-Trade and Commerce later that fall we again discussed it and exchanged correspondence about it. We communicated with the appropriate government officials in the maritime provinces and there was some difference of opinion with regard to price of pit props from the mari-times. The market had in part been lost to Russia or Finland but we did everything in our power to re-open it. I do not know the situation at the present moment.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: What about pulp wood?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Well I have no answer with regard to pulpwood. That was not discussed at the time and here is a case where statistics would be helpful as to exports of that commodity.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The minister must surely know that in past years we had a considerable market for pulpwood in France and in Great Britain. We have apparently completely lost these markets and the same would apply to long lumber. Considerable quantities of long lumber were exported from the maritime provinces, particularly eastern New Brunswick, to Great Britain and Ireland. I do not have the statistics so I am in the same position as the minister at this time, but I am given to understand that the exports of long lumber to the European market have been practically nil since the first of this year.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I will have to look into the matter and will give an answer to my hon. friend on some other occasion.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia. We should do whatever we can, and I am sure the minister agrees with this, to develop our trade in all markets, including our trade in non-strategic goods with communist countries such as China and Russia. It is true that the development of such trade is now being affected by the Soviet economic policy of forcing goods on world markets, perhaps in some cases for other than economic reasons. Experience in Europe during recent months has shown that with respect to commodities such as lumber, pulp, aluminum, oil and rails, they are putting these goods into European markets at a price with which we on this side cannot compete. It is also true that recent experience has shown, on the other hand, that they are asking too high a price for some of their exports to European markets and are not getting those markets, all of which indicates-and of course this is not new to any member of the house- that the impetus behind their trading offensive, if you can call it that, is political rather than economic. As a matter of fact, Mr. Khrushchev himself, in 1955, talking to a group of United States congressmen visiting

Moscow, said: "We value trade least for economic reasons and most for political purposes". Mr. Khrushchev has a habit, very often, of blurting out the truth.
Perhaps at the present moment, more important than the development of our trade with communist countries are the steps that might be taken to increase our trade with those countries that cannot trade with us now because of what the economists call insufficient international liquidity, which is a horrendous phrase meaning that these countries have not got enough foreign exchange to buy from us what they would like. There has been a good deal of discussion in the United States and in the United Kingdom as to what could be done to remove the consequences of this insufficiency of liquidity and help these countries get foreign exchange. Mr. Macmillan, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, has been making proposals to Washington and, perhaps, to Ottawa, also with this in mind, and the minister will recall that Dean Acheson and Adlai Stevenson both put forward some every imaginative proposals in the United States about the way in which that government could make a contribution to this end, and without United States participation it would, of course, be difficult to make progress.
Whether this can be done through existing institutions such as the international monetary fund or whether some new agency should be set up, I do not know, but I am sure the minister would agree that nothing in this field is of greater importance than to join with other countries in a new move designed to increase the purchasing capacity of these countries. I wonder whether the minister could report on any developments that may have taken place in this field since the visit of President Eisenhower or of Mr. Macmillan.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not able to make any report with regard to these matters, but the subjects raised now by the Leader of the Opposition quite naturally are being considered.
The Leader of the Opposition has correctly assessed the situation as I see it, and I hope that the international monetary fund may be strengthened, or some new organization created to strengthen this aspect of world trade. The Leader of the Opposition will fully appreciate that it is no more possible for me to make a report at this stage of the proceedings than it frequently was for him in the past on negotiations being carried on with various countries.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I was wondering whether there had been any specific proposal made either to the United States government or to the United Kingdom government, or both.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Not at this stage. It will be interesting if someone does come forward with some definite proposal.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: While we are on the subject of imports and exports, yesterday the minister, as quoted on page 2322 of Hansard, said that last year our imports from the United States were valued at approximately $4 billion. I wonder if the minister could give us any indication what it is expected that our imports in 1958 may be. I know he has stated there is going to be a decline.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I welcome the hon. member to the discussion of the trade and commerce estimates. He is coming fresh to the fray. I hope he is not too vigorous, because we have been going on a long time. I think the information he requires is contained in publications. Reports are published which give the information with regard to exports and imports, and they are available to all members. By a process of elimination I have found my copy among the other papers in front of me. I have one dealing with exports, published by the dominion bureau of statistics, and there is a companion volume headed "Imports" which gives all the relevant information from January to the end of April. That, I think, is the answer to the hon. member's question.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I also have these reports. May I point out to the minister that the reports are always based on what has taken place, and my question to him was whether he can give to the country any indication-and after all he does have these forecasters in his department-of the kind of decline in imports we may be expecting this year. Last year we bought goods worth $4,000 million. Is he able to say that this year the figure is likely to be 25 per cent less, or $1,000 million less?
I have a further question to ask the minister at this time. Is he able to indicate which areas are affected by the decline? Is it likely to be a decline in capital goods, or is it more likely to be a decline in our imports of consumer goods? I have particular reasons for asking this question, and I hope the minister will indicate both the expected size of the decline and the field in which it will occur.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
In answer to the first part of the hon. member's question, I am not in a position to forecast as he would like me to do. Forecasts are sometimes accurate, sometimes inaccurate. Economists all across the country make them from time to time, and their forecasts appear in the papers. If the hon. member wants a longer distance forecast he might refer to the reports given to the Canadian royal commission on economic prospects with regard to imports and exports.
Supply-Trade and Commerce The crystal ball has been examined there and the vista extended over a great many years.
With regard to the second part of the question, the fields in which there is a decline, here again I have to refer to these booklets and statistics which indicate Canada's import and export figures. As I pointed out yesterday, and as hon. members opposite pointed out, the decline has been to a certain extent in capital goods, and the decline in our exports has been in our primary and semi-processed metals, in some minerals and things of that nature.
There are certain downs in some things and ups in others. I have a list in front of me indicating our exports divided into half a dozen different main headings showing the general situation, but without going into very great detail I could not answer the hon. member's question. It would require reading out a great number of headings and providing statistical tables.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
In that case I have to explain to the minister my reason for asking for the information. All of us were very pleased to hear of the determination of the government to do something about eliminating our adverse trade balance with the United States. Some of us were a little alarmed at some of the methods that were proposed. Now we are indeed bringing about a closer equilibrium between our imports and our exports. However, if the reduction in our imports is as a result of a reduction in imports of capital goods, well it merely means that the expansion and the rapid industrialization that I sometimes thought was rather excessive in some years gone by is declining, and as long as we have apparent surpluses here I do not think that that alone ought to worry us overly much.
My concern is that very much of this heavy reduction in our imports may be in the field of consumer goods, and if the reduction is in the field of consumer goods then this adjusting of our adverse trade balance is happening in a manner that the Canadian people do not like and did not expect. I am asking the minister whether the plight of our unemployed who are unable to buy many of the consumer goods they would like to buy and the low income of our farmers and fishermen in Canada are the factors primarily responsible for the great decline in imports, because if that is the case then I feel we have very little that we can brag about when we say that our former adverse trade balance is not as great as it was.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I think the hon. member was otherwise engaged this afternoon when I was discussing the decline in our imports.

Supply-Trade and Commerce I pointed out that that might very well be balanced off by an increase in manufacturing in Canada. Consequently it is not necessarily a bad thing that imports should fall off if at the same time you are able to provide in Canada those materials which formerly you were importing. But I note here in some notes that I have in front of me that the decline in imports has been concentrated primarily in iron and steel and industrial machinery purchases, so that I think my hon. friend is unduly alarmed if he thinks it is just in consumer goods. I doubt very much whether he could relate the decline in those imports to any decrease in the purchasing power of the Canadian people.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, prior to June 10, 1957 and, more so, prior to March 31 of this year we heard a lot about the great decentralization program of the present government. In view of the events that are taking place in the maritime provinces, such as the announcement that a sugar plant in Saint John may be moved to central Canada and that a candy manufacturer in St. Stephen would like to follow suit and that base metal mines in northern New Brunswick are closed down completely and the coal mines have curtailed their operations at least for a period of five weeks at the present time and our pulp mills have cut down their operations from five days to three days a week, can the minister give us some clarification of the decentralization policy of this government?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: My hon. friend has been painting a picture of gloom-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Actual facts.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
-and has not mentioned some of the constructive policies of this government to put those mines back into production and to keep the coal mines functioning. Why must the hon. member just give one side of the picture?
With regard to decentralization of industry, this is something which has been advocated by this party over many years. In so far as it is possible steps will be taken to make each sector of our country prosperous and if that can be done through decentralization of industry, why steps along that line of course will be taken.
The very fact that support is being given to the coal mining industry in the maritimes is an indication of the desire of this government to maintain economic strength in that part of our country and that, of course, is part of decentralization. If they were permitted to close down and industries based on coal then shifted to central Canada you would have much greater centralization of industry than would be advantageous for Canada as a whole.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the point raised by the hon. member for Gloucester, the minister perhaps did not pay as much attention, as did the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and some other hon. members, to the famous Moncton manifesto of the Conservative party which was issued some time before the election of June 10 and which indicated that the government would set up a special agency for the promotion, not the preservation at the last minute and after a five-weeks layoff in the existing coal mines, but of new industries in the maritime provinces.
The other day I asked the leader of the house to which minister one should address questions to about this matter, and he just looked confused, and I addressed the question to the Prime Minister who was not able to give a very satisfactory answer. I wondered whether the prime responsibility for the promotion of new industries in the Atlantic provinces rested with the Department of Trade and Commerce or, if it did not, to what department's estimates it would be appropriate for us to make our inquiries.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: So far as I know, Mr. Chairman, all inquiries may be made on these estimates. If, as sometimes happens, an inquiry runs over two or three departments, I think I heard the Prime Minister say the other day that it would be quite appropriate to inquire of him.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Perhaps the minister did not quite comprehend my question. It was our understanding-I think it was the understanding of the people in the Atlantic provinces and perhaps part of the reason why the government got as much support as it did-that the government was going to set up some special agency in some particular department to take special charge of this function and I wondered whether that department was the Department of Trade and Commerce or whether it was some other department.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I have not been notified
to that effect yet.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I want to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question which has nothing to do with what we have been discussing. At the present time there is a royal commission on patents which is studying the Patent Act and the effects of the Patent Act. I was wondering whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce, through his economic adviser, has been in touch with this commission and has made representations to it? The point is this. The origin of the things which we buy is governed in many instances by the owner of the patent which

this country grants and, as the minister probably knows, about 85 per cent of the patents issued in any year are issued to foreign countries. Now, of course, there is no provision in the act to manufacture in Canada and patents generally, as the minister knows, create a monopoly and, of course, control prices. Without going into the question in detail, I was wondering whether the minister should not have his economic advisers get in touch with this commission immediately and study the effect of patents on the economy of Canada.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Was that in the order of
reference?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It has not been done.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It was not in the order of reference and your government set up the commission.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I appreciate this interjection by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration but she was also secretary of state for a while and had an opportunity to do these things. I am not reproaching her or anybody else. I am not here to reproach anybody. I am trying to do something for the citizens of this country. If there is one member of the house who has been very mild in criticism at all times in the past it is myself. At no time have I ever tried to interject anything that could be taken as a reproach upon anybody in the house. I am just requesting very nicely that the Minister of Trade and Commerce have his economic advisors consult with this commission to find out what is the effect of patents on trade and commerce in this country.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If I may, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has been interested in this question for a long time. This commission was set up at a time when his party formed the government. If my memory serves me well, the hon. member made repeated representations to his own government and to his own minister in charge of that department. I would suggest that the time when he should have made his heated criticisms was when his own minister sat on this side of the house and not now-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Well-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Now, sit down and take it-at a time when as he well knows, if he knows his law as I think he does-

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Who is in power now?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
-the order of reference cannot well be changed with respect to a commission that has been operating for three years.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I forgive the dear lady for all she has said. I am sure she does not understand. I did not start my remarks in that manner and I am just asking the minister to do something now. I am not reproaching anybody. This is a very important matter and as the commission is still functioning and has not submitted its report there is still time to do this. When the report is completed the government will no doubt look at it. Nobody has criticized anybody. This is a most innocent suggestion but probably one of the most constructive that has been made in relation to patents for some time.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: The hon. member has asked me if I will refer the matter to the economists in the Department of Trade and Commerce to see if there is anything that may be done with regard to patents in so far as they affect trade and commerce in this country. The Department of Trade and Commerce has very competent economists. I will put the problem to them and see what the answer is.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY

In so far as the pipe line being built through northern Ontario is concerned, there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction from the point of view of the municipalities which are to be served by the secondary trunk line. On numerous occasions there have been requests from the municipalities that the trans-Canada pipe line be put under public ownership. Recently, the heads of the municipalities throughout Ontario met and unanimously endorsed this position.
I think it is generally conceded by the people in northern Ontario living in the section through which the crown-controlled corporation has been operating that the crown-controlled operation has been advantageous. The farmers in that area have received much more satisfaction than those who live in the sections through which the privately owned pipe line is passing. The advantages of the crown corporation operation have been reflected in better terms for labour and better terms of expropriation.
One clause in the agreement between the crown corporation and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines gives the latter the opportunity of purchasing this line, and gives to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines the right to transmit gas through the crown corporation section of the line, and to receive any moneys that accrue from that for a period of 10 years. At the end of 10 years the private corporation has the option of buying this section at cost. At the end of that time, the crown corporation may go out of existence if the government is foolish enough to allow that to happen. Then we will find that rates will have been established for the distributing lines throughout Ontario.
The federal government could exert a great deal of influence and could assist greatly in the maintenance of fair and reasonable prices for the transmission of this gas. Unfortunately, in areas like Timmins the rates that are being quoted are $1 higher than they are 500 miles farther along that line. The people of northern Ontario are of the opinion that

Certainly the fact that the federal government did get involved in the construction of this most difficult section of the line-a fact which resulted in the line being built in Canada-has shown the Canadian people that governments can build these lines. It has been suggested in the Ontario legislature that legislation must be introduced to exercise some control over the price of the product in these distribution lines. We have seen, particularly in the sections of the line not controlled by the crown, intimidation used in connection with expropriation. Farmers have been told that if they do not sell the land the company will take them to court and expropriate it. Farmer has been set against farmer, and very little care has been exercised to ensure that a farmer knows what kind of contract he is signing. Some legislation should be introduced which would be much more acceptable to the people of the rural communities when it comes to this matter of obtaining land which the farmer may not be too happy to sell at the price which is being offered.
It would appear to me that the old Railway Act or the sections of the Pipe Lines Act which provide for expropriation are cumbersome, expensive and of a type that works in favour of the company rather than the farmer who is trying to get a fair and reasonable price for the land he has to sell.
